IRS rules under Sections 162 and 263 govern whether spending is capitalised (depreciated over years) or expensed immediately. The line between Capital Expenditure and Operating Expenses changes both tax treatment and reported NOI. See Cap-Ex for the practical roster of which property items qualify and how Replacement Reserves fund them in stabilised property.

plain: The profit when you sell a property for more than what you paid plus improvements — taxed at federal long-term rates after one year.
snappy: Profit on sale of property; long-term rates apply after one year held.
detail: Capital gain equals sale price minus selling costs minus cost basis (purchase price plus capitalised improvements). Held over a year, long-term capital-gains rates apply (0%, 15%, or 20% federal depending on income, plus state). The Section 121 primary-residence exclusion shelters up to $250K of gain ($500K married) for owners who lived in the property 2 of the past 5 years. Investment property uses a 1031 Exchange to defer gain into the next property.

plain: A Lease classified as transferring ownership-like risks and rewards to the Tenant — the Tenant accounts as if buying the property over the Lease term.
snappy: Lease accounting category where the Tenant accounts as if buying the property over the term.
detail: Capital Lease (US GAAP) or Finance Lease (IFRS) treats long-Lease-term arrangements as substantially equivalent to ownership. Tests: ownership transfers at end of term, bargain purchase option, term covers majority of asset life, or present value of Lease payments equals substantially all of asset value. Effect: Tenant records the asset and corresponding liability on balance sheet, depreciates the asset, and recognises Interest expense on the liability — not Rent expense. Common in equipment leasing; rare in Commercial Real Estate (Lease terms rarely cover 75%+ of building life). Pre-2019 GAAP and Pre-IFRS-16, operating Lease was off-balance-sheet — the major reform was forcing operating Lease on-balance-sheet too.

plain: The layered structure of all the money funding a Real Estate deal — senior debt at the bottom, equity at the top, with mezzanine and preferred equity sometimes filling in between.
snappy: Layered structure of all debt and equity funding a Real Estate deal.
detail: From safest to riskiest: Senior debt (50-65% of project cost, lowest rate, first claim on cash and collateral) → Mezzanine debt (5-15%, higher rate, secured by entity rather than property) → Preferred Equity (5-15%, fixed return ahead of common equity) → Common Equity (the Sponsor and LP capital, residual claim). Each layer prices according to its risk position. Restructuring during distress works down the stack — lender forbearance, mezz capitalisation, equity wipe-out. Sophisticated capital-stack design is the heart of institutional Real Estate finance.

plain: The cross-industry term for what Real Estate calls Promote — the Sponsor's share of profits above an investor return hurdle, taxed at lower long-term Capital Gain rates.
snappy: Sponsor's share of profits above hurdles, taxed at long-term Capital Gain rates.
detail: Carried interest is the private-equity term that subsumes Real Estate's Promote, hedge-fund 20%, and venture-capital carry. Federal tax treats carry on holdings of three or more years as long-term Capital Gain — taxed at 20% rather than the 37% top ordinary rate. Many proposals to tax carry as ordinary income have failed (2016, 2017, 2021, 2022 negotiations). The TCJA tightened the rule by extending the holding-period threshold from 1 year to 3 years. Real Estate's typical 5-7 year Hold Period comfortably meets the 3-year bar.

plain: The TCJA rule requiring carried-interest holdings to be at least three years to qualify for long-term Capital Gain rates — applies to Real Estate Promote payments.
snappy: Three-year holding rule for carried interest to qualify as long-term Capital Gain.
detail: TCJA extended the carried-interest holding requirement from one year to three years effective 2018. Promote payments to Sponsors recognised in year 1, 2, or 3 trigger short-term Capital Gain (ordinary rates up to 37%). Promote in year 4+ qualifies for long-term Capital Gain rates (20% top). Most Real Estate Hold Periods comfortably exceed three years. Short-Hold strategies (BRRRR with 12-24 month flips) lose long-term treatment. Reform to extend the rule further has failed; three-year rule remains intact through 2024.

plain: Tax losses that can't be used in the current year — carried forward indefinitely to offset future income.
snappy: Unused current-year tax losses carried forward to offset future income.
detail: Real Estate generates carryforward losses through Passive Loss rules (passive losses limited to passive income), at-risk rules, and net operating losses. Passive losses suspended in the current year carry forward indefinitely and free up when (a) the taxpayer has future passive income, (b) the taxpayer materially participates, qualifies as Real Estate Professional, and converts the activity to active, or (c) the taxpayer disposes of the property in a fully taxable Sale, allowing full release of suspended losses against ordinary income. Strategic Sale timing to release suspended losses is an estate-planning technique used routinely by sophisticated Real Estate investors.

plain: The monthly bills of owning a property — Mortgage, Property Tax, insurance, utilities, upkeep.
snappy: Ongoing monthly costs of holding a property.
detail: Carrying costs include the Mortgage payment (Principal plus Interest), Property Tax, homeowners insurance, utilities, HOA dues if applicable, and routine maintenance. For investors, carrying costs are the burn during vacancy or rehab — the gap between purchase and rent commencement that has to be funded out of pocket. Cash-on-Cash Return is computed net of carrying costs.

plain: A buyer purchasing without financing contingencies — typically faster Closing, no Appraisal risk, often preferred by sellers in competitive markets.
snappy: Buyer purchasing without financing — faster Closing, no Appraisal risk.
detail: Cash Buyers dominate distressed Sales and luxury markets. Pros from seller's perspective: no financing contingency, no Appraisal contingency, no Underwriting delays, fast Closing (5-15 days possible). Cons: typically lower offer price (cash buyers expect a discount for their leverage), proof-of-funds verification, sometimes investor-related repair-as-is conditions. Cash Buyer categories: opportunistic investors, foreign buyers parking capital, downsizing retirees with proceeds from previous Sale, institutional Single-Family Rental operators (Invitation Homes, American Homes 4 Rent), wholesalers. Cash Sales were ~30-35% of US transactions through 2023-2024.

plain: A Lender-controlled account collecting property cash flows in distressed Commercial Mortgages — funds sweep daily into Lender accounts, then disburse to borrower per agreed schedule.
snappy: Lender-controlled account collecting property cash flows during Mortgage stress.
detail: Cash Management Accounts get triggered by DSCR Covenant breaches or other distress events on Commercial Mortgages. Mechanics: all property income (Rent collections, parking, other income) deposits directly into the Lender-controlled CMA. Funds disburse per cash management waterfall: Property Tax, insurance, Operating Expenses (with Lender approval on major items), debt service, mandatory reserves (Replacement Reserve, TI reserves), excess available to borrower only if covenants restored. Borrower psychological impact: loss of cash flow control, signal to investors of distress. CMA agreements heavily negotiated at Loan origination — borrower wants high covenant trigger thresholds; Lender wants low.

plain: A Commercial Loan provision sweeping excess cash flow above debt service to a Lender-controlled reserve — triggered by DSCR Covenant breach or other distress events.
snappy: Loan provision sweeping excess cash flow to Lender reserve upon covenant breach.
detail: Cash Traps activate as Commercial Mortgage covenants weaken. Common triggers: DSCR Covenant below 1.20x (typical), DSCR below 1.05x (more conservative), occupancy below 85%, major Tenant default. Effect: excess cash flow over debt service routes to Lender-controlled reserve account rather than borrower distribution. Funds released back to borrower only when covenants restore. Cash Trap is the borrower's nightmare scenario — equity returns drop to zero during stress as cash flow disappears. Sponsors fight aggressively for high covenant triggers and quick release once covenants normalise. Cash Trap provisions surge in importance during distress cycles.

plain: A Landlord-to-Tenant payment in exchange for voluntary move-out — often used in Eviction Moratorium-protected situations, distressed property purchases, and Rent-Stabilized buyouts.
snappy: Landlord payment to Tenant in exchange for voluntary move-out.
detail: Cash-for-Keys lets Landlords accelerate Tenant departure when Eviction would be slow, contested, or impossible. Typical amounts: $2,000-$10,000 in standard rental markets; $50,000-$500,000+ for Rent-Stabilized buyouts in NYC where the Tenant gives up below-market Rent worth millions in long-term value. NYC's HSTPA reforms (2019) tightened disclosure and process for Rent-Stabilized buyouts to prevent predatory practices. California requires written disclosure that Tenant has the right to refuse, plus a 30-day rescission period. Common in: distressed-property acquisitions, condo conversions, redevelopment projects, Foreclosure sales of occupied properties.

plain: Annual cash flow from a property divided by the cash you put in — your money's actual yield.
snappy: Annual pre-tax cash flow divided by initial cash invested.
detail: Cash-on-Cash Return measures the yield on the equity actually invested, not the property's total value — so it captures the leverage effect of a Mortgage. A property with a 5% Cap Rate financed at 75% LTV can produce 10%+ cash-on-cash when rents cover the debt service. Used alongside Cap Rate and IRR to evaluate income properties; favoured for its simplicity.

plain: A Refinance where the borrower replaces an existing Mortgage with a larger one — taking the difference in cash.
snappy: Refinance into a larger Mortgage with the borrower taking the difference in cash.
detail: Cash-out refis let homeowners tap built-up Equity without selling. Typical use: home improvements, debt consolidation, education, business capital, investment property purchase. Lender restrictions on combined-LTV: typically 80% for Conventional Loans, 80% for FHA Loans, 90% for VA Loans (effectively up to 100%). Higher rate than rate-term Refinance (50-75 basis points). Loan officers must disclose if the new payment exceeds the prior one. Interest deductibility under TCJA: only deductible if used for substantial home improvements, not for personal expenses.

plain: Singular form of CC&Rs — a recorded restriction on how a property can be used or modified, common in HOA and Condo neighbourhoods.
snappy: Singular form of CC&R — a Recorded property-use restriction.
detail: CC&R is the singular form of CC&Rs. Real Estate practitioners use both freely in conversation. A single CC&R might restrict paint colours, fence types, or commercial use; collectively the CC&Rs form the governing documents alongside the Condo Declaration and Bylaws. See CC&Rs for the substantive role in HOA and Condo governance, enforcement mechanisms, and Recordation requirements.

plain: The rule book of a HOA or planned community — covers what owners can do with their property and what they pay.
snappy: Recorded private rules binding every owner in a HOA community.
detail: CC&Rs are recorded with the county and run with the land — every successor owner is bound. They typically govern paint colours, fencing, parking, pet limits, short-term-rental rules, and HOA dues. CC&Rs sit alongside the HOA bylaws (governance rules) and articles (entity formation). Buyers should review CC&Rs during Due Diligence — restrictions on use, satellite dishes, or rentals can be deal-breakers. Some old CC&Rs contain unenforceable discriminatory language that survives on paper but cannot be enforced.

plain: The HOA's or Condo's process of enforcing CC&R restrictions against owners who violate — paint colours, parking, fences, additions — via fines, Liens, and ultimately legal action.
snappy: HOA/Condo process of enforcing CC&R restrictions through fines, Liens, and legal action.
detail: CC&Rs Enforcement varies sharply by HOA culture and state law. Typical escalation: written notice of violation, hearing before HOA board, fines (often $25-$200 per violation, cumulative over time), Lien filing against the property if fines unpaid, ultimately Foreclosure on the HOA Lien. Many states (California, Florida, Texas) impose limits on fine size and procedure to prevent abuse. Recent decade has seen pushback against aggressive HOAs imposing draconian fines for trivial violations (paint colours, holiday decorations, lawn maintenance). Critics: HOA enforcement creates disproportionate burdens on lower-income or non-traditional homeowners.

plain: A Senior Housing community offering all care levels on one campus — Independent Living, Assisted Living, Memory Care, Skilled Nursing — residents pay an entry fee plus monthly charges.
snappy: Senior community with all care levels on one campus and entry-fee-plus-monthly pricing.
detail: CCRC is the most complex Senior Housing subtype. Residents pay a substantial entry fee ($100,000-$1M depending on community and unit, varies on refundability) plus monthly service fees, in exchange for guaranteed access to higher-acuity care as needs change — Independent Living → Assisted Living → Memory Care → Skilled Nursing — without leaving the campus. Three contract types: Type A (Life Care, fixed monthly fee for life regardless of care level), Type B (modified contract, partial service guarantee), Type C (fee-for-service, market rates for higher care). Major operators: Acts Retirement, Erickson Living, Life Care Services, ABHM. State regulation is heavy.

plain: Standalone or rooftop infrastructure leased to wireless carriers — Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile — for cellular network coverage.
snappy: Standalone or rooftop infrastructure leased to wireless carriers for network coverage.
detail: Cell Towers are an institutional niche asset class. Operators: American Tower Corporation (largest), Crown Castle (now data-centre-focused), SBA Communications. Tower types: lattice (tall standalone), monopole (single pole), guyed wire (least common). Co-location revenue model: multiple carriers per tower paying separate rents — sweet spot is 3-4 carriers. Lease economics: 20-30 year Tenant Lease with rent escalations, generally 5-Year Lease automatic renewals. Cap Rates: 3-4% — among the tightest in Commercial Real Estate reflecting Tenant credit and barriers to construction. 5G rollout drove additional tower densification 2019-2023.

plain: The official local-government sign-off that a building is safe to live in — required before owners can move in.
snappy: Local sign-off declaring a building safe and legal to occupy.
detail: A CO is issued by the local building department after all required inspections pass — typically structural, electrical, plumbing, mechanical, and final. New construction cannot legally be occupied without one. Renovations that change the use class (converting commercial to residential) usually require a new CO. Title companies often condition Closing on the CO's issuance for new builds. Some older properties operate under grandfathered occupancy without a modern CO.

plain: The federal agency that regulates consumer mortgages and writes the rules Lenders must follow when lending to homebuyers.
snappy: US federal consumer-finance regulator overseeing Mortgages.
detail: The CFPB was created in 2010 under the Dodd-Frank Act in response to the 2008 financial crisis. It enforces consumer-finance laws including TILA and RESPA, wrote the TRID disclosure rule, and supervises non-bank Mortgage Lenders. Its complaints database and enforcement actions discipline Lenders for unfair, deceptive, or abusive practices. Borrowers can file complaints directly with the CFPB if a Lender mishandles their loan.

plain: The standard liability insurance for Commercial Real Estate — covers third-party bodily injury, property damage, and personal/advertising injury claims.
snappy: Standard liability insurance for Commercial Real Estate — third-party injury and damage.
detail: CGL is required by virtually every Commercial Real Estate Lender and Lease. Standard limits: $1M per occurrence / $2M aggregate. Coverage: slip-and-fall on the property, water damage to neighbouring property, libel/slander in Tenant marketing, contractual indemnifications. Excluded: pollution, professional services (E&O Insurance), workers compensation, liquor liability. Tenant-required CGL with Landlord as additional insured is the standard Lease requirement. Annual premium: $2,000-$30,000+.

plain: The full historical sequence of Deed transfers showing how the Title moved from owner to owner.
snappy: Sequence of recorded Deeds linking current owner back through prior owners.
detail: An unbroken chain of Title — each owner properly conveying via recorded Deed to the next — is what Title Insurance verifies before issuing a policy. A break (a missing recorded transfer, an unprobated will, a forged Deed) creates a cloud on Title that must be cured by quiet-title action, affidavit, or curative document. Chain-of-Title problems are the single most common source of Title Insurance claims.

plain: A formal amendment to a construction contract modifying scope, schedule, or price — additive or deductive — signed by both owner and GC.
snappy: Formal amendment to a construction contract modifying scope, schedule, or price.
detail: Change Orders are the contractual mechanism for handling project changes during construction. Common drivers: owner-initiated upgrades, code-required modifications, unforeseen subsurface conditions, design errors, Tenant Improvement scope changes. Each Change Order documents: scope of work changed, cost impact, schedule impact, signature requirements. Cost-plus contracts handle changes more flexibly; stipulated-sum contracts treat each change as a separate negotiation. Aggressive change-order practice by contractors (over-billing on changes) is a recurring construction-fraud pattern; owners audit change orders carefully and require detailed back-up cost documentation.

plain: Federal bankruptcy reorganisation — a debtor in distress restructures its debts and continues operating, eventually emerging with renegotiated obligations.
snappy: Federal bankruptcy reorganisation — restructure debts while continuing to operate.
detail: Chapter 11 lets Real Estate-heavy debtors (Hotels, Retail chains, Office building owners) restructure while preserving operating value. Debtor files petition; automatic stay halts creditor actions; court oversees plan of reorganisation. Property: typically retained by debtor; rejected Leases discharged; modified Leases continue. Cramdown lets the court approve plans over creditor objection if 'fair and equitable'. Notable Real Estate Chapter 11s: General Growth Properties (2009), Toys R Us (2017-2018), Bed Bath & Beyond (2023). Distinct from Chapter 7 (liquidation).

plain: Federal bankruptcy liquidation — a debtor's assets are sold and proceeds distributed to creditors — the debtor entity ceases to exist.
snappy: Federal bankruptcy liquidation — assets sold, proceeds distributed, entity ceases.
detail: Chapter 7 is the liquidation flavour of bankruptcy. Trustee appointed to liquidate debtor's assets; proceeds distributed to creditors per statutory priority (secured creditors first, then priority unsecured, then general unsecured). Real Estate held by Chapter 7 debtors typically sells at 363 Sales (court-approved auctions). Distinct from Chapter 11 (reorganisation while continuing operations). Common in: small-business Chapter 7s where reorganisation is unviable, individual consumer bankruptcies (most US bankruptcies). Real Estate ownership generally cannot continue post-Chapter 7 — Trustee Sales the property.

plain: A Mortgage secured by Personal Property — most commonly the manufactured home itself — rather than Real Property — common in Mobile Home Park settings.
snappy: Mortgage secured by Personal Property (typically the Manufactured Home), not Real Property.
detail: Chattel Mortgages dominate Manufactured Home financing where the home sits on rented Land. Federal HMDA reporting separately tracks chattel-only Manufactured Home loans. Interest rates: 200-400 basis points higher than conventional Mortgages on Manufactured Homes financed as Real Property. Loan terms shorter (10-20 years versus 30). FHA Title I and USDA programs offer chattel-loan guarantees in eligible markets. Critics: chattel financing in Mobile Home Parks creates vulnerability.

plain: The HUD successor to HOPE VI — funds comprehensive neighbourhood revitalisation around distressed public housing — broader scope than housing-only.
snappy: HUD successor to HOPE VI funding comprehensive neighbourhood revitalisation.
detail: Choice Neighborhoods (created 2010) coordinates HUD investment with educational, transit, health, and community-service investments. Implementation Grants up to $50M fund neighbourhood transformation; smaller Planning Grants fund pre-grant strategy. Notable projects: Eastside Heritage (Atlanta), Yesler Terrace (Seattle), Iberville (New Orleans). The program emphasises permanent affordability covenants. Funding through annual congressional appropriations.

plain: A state-created insurance company providing Homeowners Insurance in markets where private insurers won't write — Florida's is the largest, covering hurricane and flood risk many private carriers exit.
snappy: State-run insurer of last resort for properties private carriers won't cover.
detail: Florida's Citizens Property Insurance Corporation, created in 2002, is the prototype. It writes Homeowners Insurance in coastal and high-risk areas where private carriers withdraw — and has grown to roughly 1.4 million policies (2024) amid hurricane-driven private-market collapse. California FAIR Plan is the wildfire equivalent (~250,000 policies, growing). Louisiana Citizens, Texas Windstorm Insurance Association similar. Premiums are state-set, often below true risk-adjusted price; deficits trigger assessments on all in-state property-insurance policyholders. Insurance of last resort by design — broader, deeper, costlier coverage than private market.

plain: The highest grade of commercial property — newest, best-located, premium finishes, top rents and lowest vacancy.
snappy: Top grade of commercial property — newest, best-located, premium rents.
detail: Class A property anchors institutional portfolios. Defined relative to local market: a Class A building in suburban Phoenix differs from a Class A in midtown Manhattan. Common attributes: built or substantially renovated in the last 15-20 years, prime location with strong access, full amenity package, blue-chip tenant roster, premium asking Rent (top quartile of submarket). Class A trades at the tightest Cap Rates because risk is lowest. Pension funds, sovereign wealth, and listed REITs concentrate here.

plain: The middle grade of commercial property — older but well-maintained, decent locations, market-average rents.
snappy: Middle grade of commercial property — older, well-kept, market-rate Rents.
detail: Class B is where most US Commercial Real Estate sits. Buildings 20-40 years old, dated finishes, functional but unspectacular. Cap Rates trade 75-150 basis points wider than Class A for the same submarket. Value-add Sponsors target Class B for renovation to lift NOI toward Class A pricing — light Rehab on common areas, unit interiors, mechanical systems. Class B office took the biggest 2020-2023 occupancy hit as Class A absorbed flight-to-quality demand.

plain: The lower grade of commercial property — older, deferred maintenance, secondary locations, below-market Rents.
snappy: Lower grade of commercial property — older, sometimes deferred-maintenance, below-market rents.
detail: Class C property earns the widest Cap Rates and the highest yield-on-cost — at the cost of higher Tenant turnover, more management intensity, and meaningful Cap-Ex needs. Often 40+ years old with deferred maintenance, functional obsolescence, and locations away from prime corridors. Workforce-housing Multifamily and value-add Class C office are common Sponsor strategies. Class C suffers most in down cycles and recovers slowest in up cycles. Lender appetite is thinner — bridge debt and Hard Money fill more of the capital stack.

plain: The vertical distance from the floor to the lowest hanging object inside an Industrial building — drives storage capacity per square foot.
snappy: Industrial building vertical clearance from floor to lowest hanging object.
detail: Clear Height drives Industrial property economics. Old (pre-1980) warehouses: 18-22 foot clear. Modern bulk warehouses: 32-40+ foot clear. The taller the clear, the more pallet positions per square foot using vertical racking. Amazon-style fulfilment centres demand 36-40 foot clear; e-commerce-grade modern bulk space trades at substantial Rent premium over older warehouses. Cross-Dock facilities have varying clear heights by zone. Specialty: cold storage requires lower clear heights (16-22 foot typical) due to refrigeration costs and operational constraints. Clear Height plus Truck Court depth are the two structural variables driving Industrial Rent per square foot.

plain: The final step of a property sale where the Deed transfers and money changes hands.
snappy: Settlement meeting where ownership transfers and funds settle.
detail: At Closing the seller signs the Deed, the buyer signs the Mortgage and note, Escrow releases funds, Title Insurance attaches, and the Deed is recorded with the county. Closing also marks settlement of Closing Costs, prorated Property Tax, and remaining Earnest Money Deposit credits. Increasingly handled remotely with e-signatures and remote online notarisation. Also called settlement or completion depending on the region.

plain: All the fees you pay at the finish line of a home purchase — usually 2-5% of the price on top of the Down Payment.
snappy: Bundle of fees and prepaid items paid at Closing, separate from purchase price.
detail: Closing costs include Lender fees (origination, Underwriting, Appraisal), third-party fees (Title Insurance, Escrow, recording), prepaid items (Property Tax, insurance, Mortgage Interest), and government taxes. Buyers pay 2-5% of price in most US markets. The Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure (TRID forms) itemise every charge. Sellers can be asked to cover some closing costs as a negotiation concession.

plain: The final paperwork the Lender must give you three days before Closing, listing every cost and term.
snappy: required by TRID form detailing final loan terms and Closing Costs.
detail: The Closing Disclosure replaced the HUD-1 Settlement Statement under TRID rules in 2015. Lenders must deliver it at least three business days before Closing so borrowers have time to verify costs against the earlier Loan Estimate. Material changes (different APR, different loan product, prepayment penalty added) reset the three-day clock. The form covers interest rate, monthly payment, every Closing Cost line item, and cash-to-close.

plain: A letter — issued by the Title Insurer — protecting the Lender from specific Title Agent errors or fraud during Closing, like wire-fund mishandling.
snappy: Title Insurer letter protecting Lender from Title Agent errors during Closing.
detail: Closing Protection Letters protect Lenders from Title Agent errors. Coverage: theft or misappropriation of Closing funds by the Title Agent, failure to follow the Lender's Closing instructions, certain Title Defects discovered post-Closing. The CPL is issued by the Title Insurer underwriting the policy, not the Title Company conducting the Closing. Cost: $25-$50 per transaction. Required by virtually every residential Mortgage Lender. CPL is the primary insurance source recovering from Wire Fraud at the Title Company level — though specific limitations and exclusions apply.

plain: A pending claim or defect that makes Title less than marketable — anything from an unreleased Lien to a heir contesting Probate to a forged Deed in the chain.
snappy: Pending claim or defect that makes Title less than marketable.
detail: Clouds on title surface in title searches: unreleased Mortgages from prior owners, Liens that never got removed, deceased owners whose interest never transferred, forgeries, Adverse Possession claims, missing signatures on historical Deeds, recordings under wrong legal description. Curing a cloud might mean: tracking down a prior owner for a release, filing Quitclaim Deeds from heirs, court-ordered Quiet Title actions, statutory cure proceedings. Title Insurance covers some clouds the title search missed; uncured clouds disclosed at Closing typically delay or kill the transaction.

plain: Bonds backed by pools of Commercial Real Estate mortgages — investors get paid from the rent and Principal of the underlying buildings.
snappy: Bonds backed by pools of Commercial Real Estate mortgages.
detail: CMBS bundle Commercial Mortgages on office, retail, industrial, hotel, and Multifamily property into tranched securities sold to institutional investors. Senior tranches (AAA) absorb losses last; junior tranches (BB and below) absorb first. Loans inside CMBS are typically 10-year, fixed-rate, non-recourse, with strict prepayment penalties (defeasance or yield maintenance). Issuance peaked pre-2008, collapsed, recovered, and softened again post-2020 as office vacancies stressed legacy pools. Special servicers handle workouts when borrowers default.

plain: A capital partner taking a GP economic stake alongside the primary Sponsor — typically larger LP commitments earn co-GP economics including Promote participation.
snappy: Capital partner taking GP economics alongside the primary Sponsor.
detail: Co-GP structures emerged in the 2010s as institutional LPs sought alignment beyond pure-LP economics. The capital partner commits LP capital plus an additional smaller commitment to the GP entity — gaining a share of the Sponsor's Promote and asset-management fees. Co-GP economics: typically 25-50% of Sponsor Promote in exchange for 10-25% of GP-level capital. Major institutional players in co-GP: Goldman Sachs's Real Estate Principal Investment Area, KKR, Brookfield, Blackstone. Pros for Sponsor: lower capital requirement, deeper relationship. Cons: dilution of Promote, additional governance to manage.

plain: An insurance contract provision requiring the policyholder to insure the property to a specified percentage of value — typically 80% — or face a penalty proportional to underinsurance.
snappy: Insurance provision requiring coverage to a specified percentage of value, or penalty applies.
detail: Co-Insurance penalises underinsured policyholders. Typical clause: 80% Co-Insurance — policyholder must insure to at least 80% of property replacement cost. If actual coverage falls below the threshold, claim payment is reduced proportionally. Example: property worth $1M, 80% Co-Insurance requires $800K coverage; if owner insures to only $400K, claims pay 50% of loss (400K/800K = 50% Co-Insurance fulfillment). Co-Insurance is common on commercial property; agreed-value or eliminated-coinsurance endorsements are available at higher premium. Policyholders must update coverage as property values rise.

plain: A building where owners hold shares in a corporation that owns the whole building, rather than owning their unit individually.
snappy: Building owned by a corporation; residents own shares plus a proprietary lease.
detail: Distinct from a Condo: a co-op shareholder doesn't own real estate at all — they own shares in the corporation that owns the building, plus a proprietary lease to a specific apartment. Co-op boards screen buyers, often rejecting applicants for opaque reasons. Financing is harder (many Lenders don't lend on co-ops; share loans replace Mortgages). Common in NYC where ~75% of pre-war buildings are co-ops; rare elsewhere.

plain: The process of turning a rental Multifamily building in NYC and other co-op-heavy markets into a cooperative corporation with shareholder-owners — historically dominant pre-1990s.
snappy: Process converting a rental Multifamily into a cooperative corporation with shareholder-owners.
detail: Co-op conversion was the dominant urban Multifamily-to-ownership conversion in NYC and a few other markets through the 1970s-1990s. Two flavours: eviction-plan conversion (Tenants forced to buy or vacate — used widely 1979-1985 then largely banned in NYC) and non-eviction-plan conversion (Tenants get insider price and right to stay as renters, but can buy at retail). NYC Martin Act regulates conversion offerings, requiring detailed offering plans approved by the AG. The shift from Condo Conversion in newer markets reflects co-op's specific NYC dominance; Condo is the national default elsewhere.

plain: A Lease provision letting Tenants reduce Rent or break their Lease if a key Anchor or specified Co-Tenant leaves the Retail centre — protects inline Tenants from traffic collapse.
snappy: Lease provision letting Tenants cut Rent or exit if a key Co-Tenant leaves.
detail: Co-Tenancy Clauses are the inline Tenant's protection against centre decline. Opening co-tenancy: Tenant doesn't have to open if specified anchors aren't operating at centre opening. Operating co-tenancy: Tenant can pay reduced Rent (often 50%) or terminate if Anchor occupancy drops below a threshold (typically 70% or specific anchors closing). Triggered: department-store bankruptcy waves (Macy's, JCPenney closures), grocery-store exits, big-box failures. Landlords push back with replacement-Anchor windows and substitution rights. Co-Tenancy litigation is common — what counts as 'open and operating' surfaces interpretive disputes.

plain: Another Tenant in the same Retail centre or Multifamily property — Co-Tenants share Common Areas and may have rights tied to each other under Co-Tenancy Clauses.
snappy: Other Tenants in the same centre — Co-Tenant rights flow from Co-Tenancy Clauses.
detail: Co-Tenant is the umbrella term for any other Tenant in the same property — Retail centre, Office building, Multifamily, mixed-use. Each Tenant's Lease may reference Co-Tenants directly via Co-Tenancy Clauses (linking Rent reductions or termination rights to specific Co-Tenant occupancy). Co-Tenants share Common Area Maintenance pro-rata, Common Areas, and exposure to building-wide issues (parking, security, signage). Disputes between Co-Tenants over noise, smells, and Common Area use surface in commercial Property Management routinely.

plain: An Industrial property with refrigerated and frozen storage capacity — different building specs than conventional warehouse, with high construction and operating costs.
snappy: Industrial property with refrigerated and frozen storage capacity.
detail: Cold Storage occupies a specialised Industrial niche. Construction costs 2-3x conventional warehouse — insulation, refrigeration equipment, fast-roll doors, specialised flooring. Operating costs likewise high — refrigeration is a power-hungry, 24/7 demand. Cap Rates 100-200 bps wider than conventional Industrial. Demand structurally growing with e-commerce grocery (Instacart, Amazon Fresh, Walmart Grocery), meal-kit delivery, frozen-food e-commerce. Major operators: Lineage Logistics (largest, private), Americold (listed REIT), United States Cold Storage. Build-to-Suit Cold Storage development is hot — Tenant credit and 20-year Lease commitments justify the substantial development cost premium.

plain: Apparent legal ownership based on a written document — even if that document is technically defective — supports Adverse Possession claims with shorter statutory periods.
snappy: Apparent ownership from a written Deed even if defective — supports faster Adverse Possession.
detail: Color of Title arises when a party holds a written document purporting to convey Real Property — but the document is defective. Examples: Deed from someone who didn't actually own the property; forged signature in the chain; legal description omits part of the property. The holder believes they own; their possession looks like ownership. Many states grant Color of Title holders shorter Adverse Possession periods (5-7 years) than required without (15-20+ years), reflecting that they were acting in good faith from a recorded document. Color of Title also expands the area claimed under Adverse Possession to the full scope of the Deed's description.

plain: Income-producing real estate — offices, retail, industrial, hotels, multifamily — bought to generate rent rather than to live in.
snappy: Income-producing real estate held as investment rather than primary residence.
detail: Commercial Real Estate spans office, retail, industrial, multifamily (5+ units), hospitality, and specialty segments — anything held for rental income or investment return. CRE financing, valuation (Cap Rate, NOI, DSCR), Underwriting standards, and Leasing structures differ materially from residential. Owners are typically LLCs or partnerships rather than individuals; transactions involve longer Due Diligence and more sophisticated counsel.

plain: The percentage of the sale price paid to real estate agents at Closing — historically 5-6% split between buyer and listing sides.
snappy: Percentage of sale price paid to real estate agents at Closing.
detail: Real estate Commission is paid by the seller out of sale proceeds, traditionally 5-6% split between the listing agent and the Buyer's Agent. The 2024 NAR settlement decoupled Commission from the MLS — buyers and their agents now sign written representation agreements with explicit Commission terms before tours, and the listing no longer advertises a buy-side Commission. Effects on average Commission rates are still settling out as of 2026.

plain: Parts of a Condo or planned community that everyone owns and shares — lobbies, pools, roofs, hallways.
snappy: Shared portions of a Condo or planned community.
detail: Common Areas in a Condo include hallways, lobbies, elevators, the roof, exterior walls, mechanical rooms, and amenities. Each unit owner holds an undivided fractional interest in the Common Area alongside fee-simple ownership of their unit. The HOA maintains Common Areas and funds them via owner dues. Limited Common Areas (a balcony, parking space, storage unit) are common areas assigned to one unit's exclusive use.

plain: In nine states, anything either spouse earns or buys during marriage is owned 50/50 — separately tracked from pre-marital or inherited property.
snappy: Marital-property regime in nine states treating earnings during marriage as 50/50 owned.
detail: Community Property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, Wisconsin. (Alaska, Tennessee, and a few others permit opt-in.) Anything acquired during marriage is community property regardless of titling; pre-marital property and inheritances remain separate. At death of one spouse, the survivor receives a full step-up in basis on the entire community-property home (versus 50% step-up in common-law states) — a major federal income-tax advantage. Divorce courts split community property equally.

plain: A recently sold home similar to yours, used as evidence of what your home is worth.
snappy: Recently sold property similar in size, location, and features — anchors a valuation.
detail: Comps are the working currency of real estate valuation. Appraisers, agents, and investors pull three to six recently closed sales of similar properties within roughly a mile and adjust for differences in square footage, lot, bedrooms, condition, and view to estimate subject value. The sales comparison approach dominates residential Appraisal; commercial Appraisal uses income and cost approaches alongside it.

plain: A Hotel's defined group of 3-7 competitor properties used for performance benchmarking — track ADR, Occupancy Rate, and RevPAR relative to peers.
snappy: Hotel's benchmark group of 3-7 competitors for ADR, Occupancy, RevPAR comparison.
detail: Comp Set is the operating benchmark for Hotel performance. STR (now CoStar Group) provides comp-set reports comparing the subject Hotel's ADR, Occupancy Rate, and RevPAR to the average of designated competitors. RGI (RevPAR Generation Index): subject RevPAR ÷ comp set RevPAR × 100; above 100 means outperformance, below means underperformance. ARI (ADR Index) and MPI (Market Penetration Index for Occupancy) similar. Hotel asset managers track weekly STR reports closely. Choosing the Comp Set is itself political — including weaker competitors flatters the subject Hotel's relative performance. Brand standards require submission to brand-defined Comp Sets.

plain: A real estate Agent's informal valuation of a property — uses recent Sales of comparable homes to estimate likely Sale Price, simpler than a formal Appraisal.
snappy: Agent's informal valuation using recent comparable sales — simpler than a formal Appraisal.
detail: CMA is the standard listing-pricing tool. Agents pull 5-10 recently sold Comps from the MLS, adjust for differences (square footage, condition, lot size, features), and produce a likely Sale Price range. Distinct from an Appraisal: a CMA is not an Appraiser's formal opinion, isn't USPAP-compliant, can't satisfy lender Underwriting. But CMAs run free (part of the listing service), are produced in days, and are more current than Appraisals (which lag market shifts). Sellers use CMAs to set list price; buyers use CMAs to gauge whether a list price is reasonable.

plain: Free or discounted Rent and other incentives Landlords offer to attract Tenants — months free, reduced Security Deposit, gift cards, TI allowances above market.
snappy: Discounts or freebies Landlords offer to attract Tenants — months free, reduced deposit, TI bumps.
detail: Concessions surge in soft Lease-up markets and disappear in tight ones. Multifamily: 1-2 months free on a 12-month Lease is a typical recession-era concession (effectively 8-17% Rent discount net of the free months). Office and Retail: above-market Tenant Improvement allowances, free Rent periods of 6-12+ months on long Leases. Economic occupancy distinguishes properties running market-rate Rent from those papering over with concessions — physical occupancy can be 95% while effective occupancy is 80%. Underwriting models 'effective Rent' net of concessions, not 'face Rent'.

plain: A Lender's commitment to fund a Mortgage subject to specific conditions — typically Appraisal, Title clearance, employment verification — issued after underwriting.
snappy: Lender Mortgage commitment subject to specific conditions like Appraisal and Title clearance.
detail: Conditional Approval comes after the Lender has fully underwritten the borrower. Conditions typically include: satisfactory Appraisal, clean Title commitment, current employment verification, no material credit changes, asset documentation. Distinct from Pre-Approval (preliminary, pre-property) and Clear-to-Close (final approval). Timeline from Conditional Approval to Closing: typically 7-21 days. Most conditions are routine; significant delays come from Appraisal coming in low, Title issues requiring curing, or borrower employment changes. Strong Conditional Approval letter is the gold standard for offer credibility in competitive markets.

plain: A Lien Waiver effective only when the corresponding payment actually clears — protects contractors against bounced checks while still giving owners progress-payment protection.
snappy: Lien Waiver effective only when the corresponding payment actually clears.
detail: Conditional Lien Waiver bridges the gap between payment-issuance and payment-clearance. The contractor signs at the moment of receiving the payment (often a check that hasn't cleared yet). The waiver is 'conditional on actual receipt of funds' — if the check bounces or the wire fails, the waiver doesn't take effect and the lien right preserves. Once the payment clears, the contractor signs an Unconditional Lien Waiver. State-specific forms exist for both. California (Civil Code §8132-§8138) has the most prescribed statutory forms. Failure to use conditional/unconditional distinction can produce double payment exposure for owners.

plain: A Zoning approval for a use not allowed by right, but allowed if specific conditions are met — like a daycare in a residential zone.
snappy: Zoning approval for a use allowed only under specified conditions.
detail: Conditional uses are listed in the Zoning ordinance — they're permitted as of right only if the applicant can demonstrate compatibility with the neighbourhood and meet specific conditions (hours of operation, traffic mitigation, buffer landscaping, parking minimums). The local planning commission or board reviews; some jurisdictions require city council approval. Common conditional uses: schools, churches, daycares, group homes, gas stations, drive-throughs, cell towers. Granted CUPs run with the Land but can be revoked if conditions are violated.

plain: An individually owned unit inside a larger building where common areas are shared and run by an HOA.
snappy: Individually owned unit (own Deed) with shared common areas and HOA governance.
detail: Condo owners hold fee simple Title to their unit plus an undivided interest in common areas — hallways, lobby, roof, amenities. The HOA collects monthly dues to maintain common areas and enforces CC&Rs. Condos finance like single-family homes (FHA Loan and conventional both available) but Lenders also underwrite the building's financials, owner-occupancy ratio, and reserve adequacy. Contrast with a Co-op.

plain: The process of turning a rental Multifamily building into individually-owned Condo units — Tenants get the right to buy their units, then the rest sell to the open market.
snappy: Process converting a rental Multifamily into individually-owned Condo units.
detail: Condo conversion was a defining urban Real Estate move in the 1970s-1980s and revived periodically in hot markets. Local laws govern the process — Tenant protections (right of first refusal, relocation assistance, senior/disabled exemptions) vary widely. New York City and San Francisco have particularly tight rules. Economics work when Condo retail value per unit exceeds rental Sale Price by enough to cover conversion costs (legal, condo declaration, common-area renovation) and Tenant payouts. Tenants choosing not to buy must vacate or remain under rent-controlled terms depending on jurisdiction.

plain: The recorded master document that creates a Condo association — defines unit boundaries, common areas, voting rights, and the rules under which the association operates.
snappy: Recorded master document creating a Condo association and defining unit/common-area boundaries.
detail: The Condo Declaration is the foundational document, filed with the county recorder when the project is first declared as Condo. It defines: unit boundaries (often the inside surface of perimeter walls), undivided interest in common elements, limited common elements (balconies, parking, storage assigned to specific units), voting weights, restrictions on use. The Bylaws govern association operations. The CC&Rs govern owner conduct. Together, the Declaration, Bylaws, and CC&Rs form 'governing documents' a buyer must review during Due Diligence. Amendments require supermajority owner approval — 75% or higher in most states.

plain: A Mortgage small enough to meet the size limits Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will buy — most everyday US Mortgages.
snappy: Mortgage at or below the size limit Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will purchase.
detail: Conforming Loans meet underwriting and loan-size limits set annually by FHFA. The standard 2024 limit is $766,550 in most US counties, higher in designated high-cost areas. Conforming loans are routinely sold from Lenders to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, packaged into agency MBS, and resold to investors — that liquidity is why conforming rates are cheaper than jumbo. Above the limit it becomes a jumbo loan.

plain: A voluntary, permanent Easement restricting the development or use of Land — granted to a land Trust or government in exchange for an income tax deduction equal to the development-rights value.
snappy: Voluntary permanent Easement restricting development, generating tax deduction for grantor.
detail: Conservation Easements protect Land while generating tax benefits. The landowner grants restrictive Easement (no development, agricultural-only use, view preservation) to a qualified land Trust or government entity. The reduction in property value (development rights restricted) creates a federal income-tax deduction. Land Trust holders include The Nature Conservancy, regional land trusts. Tax abuse: 'syndicated conservation easements' inflate development-rights appraisals to generate paper tax losses far exceeding economic substance. IRS has aggressively pursued syndicated easements since 2020; criminal indictments multiple appraisers and promoters.

plain: A flaw in construction or materials — leaks, structural problems, code violations — that causes property damage or fails to meet contract specifications.
snappy: Flaw in construction or materials causing damage or failing contract specs.
detail: Construction Defect categories: design defects (architect or engineer error), workmanship defects (improper installation), materials defects (faulty products), code violations. Common defects: water intrusion (windows, roofs, foundations), structural settling, electrical issues, plumbing leaks, HVAC system failures, balcony or deck failures. Liability theories: breach of contract, breach of express or implied warranty, negligence, strict products liability. Multifamily and Condo construction defects can generate massive class actions — 'leaky condo' crisis devastated Florida Condo market in the 2000s-2010s. Insurance: builder's general liability, professional liability for design defects, completed-operations coverage for finished work.

plain: A short-term loan that funds the building of a new property — draws cash as the work progresses.
snappy: Short-term loan disbursing in stages to fund construction.
detail: Construction Loans fund building rather than purchase. Funds release in draws against completed milestones (foundation, framing, drywall, completion), each verified by Inspector visits. Typically 12-24 month terms with interest-only payments on the drawn balance. Higher interest rates than purchase Mortgages reflect construction risk. Construction-to-permanent (one-time-close) loans convert automatically to a standard Mortgage on completion. Builders use construction loans too — separate from end-buyer financing.

plain: Interest paid on construction debt that's capitalised into the property's Cost Basis under IRC rules — rather than deducted in the year paid — recovers through Depreciation over the building's useful life.
snappy: Interest paid during construction capitalised into Cost Basis under IRC §263A.
detail: Construction Period Interest is treated specially under tax law. IRC §263A's Uniform Capitalization Rules require capitalisation of Interest during the construction period, lengthening the Cost Basis recovery period to the building's MACRS life. Without capitalisation, Sponsors could deduct construction Interest immediately, generating large losses against other income — a tax shelter abused in pre-1986 Real Estate. Capitalised Interest applies to Substantial Completion; thereafter Mortgage Interest is currently deductible. Tax treatment differs from book treatment (some GAAP-based capitalisations are narrower). Cost Segregation studies properly account for construction-period Interest allocation across building components.

plain: A Mortgage that funds Construction during build then automatically converts to a Permanent Loan at Substantial Completion — single Closing covers both phases.
snappy: Mortgage funding construction then converting to Permanent Loan at Substantial Completion.
detail: Construction-to-Permanent Loans simplify residential and small-commercial construction financing. Mechanics: borrower signs at Closing on the combined construction-and-permanent loan; funds release in draws against milestones; at Substantial Completion the loan converts automatically to a fixed-rate Permanent Loan without re-Underwriting. Pros: one Closing, locked-in permanent rate. Cons: higher rate than separate Construction Loan + Permanent Loan. Common for Custom Homes and small Commercial owner-occupier construction.

plain: Doctrine letting a Tenant treat a Lease as terminated and vacate without owing Rent when the Landlord's serious failure to maintain the premises makes it effectively uninhabitable.
snappy: Tenant doctrine of treating Lease as terminated when Landlord fails to maintain habitability.
detail: Constructive Eviction is the Tenant's nuclear-option remedy. Requirements: Landlord substantially failed to deliver promised possession or maintain habitability (broken heat in winter, unrepaired water damage, pest infestation, security failure exposing Tenant to danger). Tenant must give written notice and reasonable time to cure. If Landlord doesn't cure, Tenant can vacate, treat Lease as terminated, and sue Landlord for damages (relocation costs, higher Rent at next location). Commercial Constructive Eviction is harder to prove — courts apply less generously than residential. Landlord defense: cure the underlying habitability issue before Tenant abandons.

plain: Legal notice imputed to a party because information is available in public records — even if the party didn't actually look — covers everything Recorded in the public-land registry.
snappy: Legal notice imputed because information is available in public records, regardless of actual knowledge.
detail: Constructive Notice is what every Recording statute creates. Once a document (Deed, Mortgage, Lien, Easement, judgment) is properly Recorded with the county recorder, every subsequent person dealing with the property is legally on notice of its contents — whether or not they actually search the records. A buyer who fails to obtain a Title search is still legally bound by recorded prior interests. Distinct from Actual Notice (genuine awareness) and Inquiry Notice (red flags should have prompted further investigation). Constructive Notice is why Title Insurance is essential — protects against defects that constructive-notice doctrine wouldn't have surfaced from a careful Title Search.

plain: A clause in a purchase contract that lets the buyer back out without losing the Earnest Money Deposit if something specific goes wrong.
snappy: Contractual escape hatch tied to a specific condition being met.
detail: Common contingencies include the inspection contingency (buyer can walk if inspection finds problems), the Appraisal Contingency (buyer can walk if the property doesn't appraise at contract price), the financing contingency (buyer can walk if the Lender denies the loan), and the home-sale contingency (buyer can walk if their existing home doesn't sell). Removing contingencies makes an offer more attractive but riskier for the buyer.

plain: A Mortgage that is not government-backed — not an FHA Loan, VA Loan, or USDA Loan. Most US Mortgages are conventional.
snappy: Non-government Mortgage; usually purchased by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac.
detail: Conventional Loans contrast with government-backed loans (FHA Loan, VA Loan, USDA). Most are Conforming Loans bought by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac; some are non-conforming jumbos held on Lender balance sheets or sold to private investors. Conventional borrowers with Down Payment under 20% pay Private Mortgage Insurance (PMI) until they reach 20% Equity. Generally requires higher Credit Score than government-backed alternatives.

plain: Roofing with high solar reflectance and emissivity — reduces building cooling loads, energy consumption, urban heat island — increasingly required by state energy codes.
snappy: Roofing with high reflectance — reduces cooling loads and energy consumption.
detail: Cool Roofs reflect more solar radiation than conventional roofs. Materials: white TPO single-ply membrane, white EPDM, light-colour modified bitumen, reflective metal roofing, specialty cool-roof shingles. Energy savings: 10-20% cooling reduction in warm climates. Initial cost: comparable to standard roofing or 5-15% premium. California Title 24 requires cool roofs on most new commercial construction and renovations. Energy Star Cool Roof certification: 65% initial reflectance, 50% after 3 years. ULP cool-roof requirements increasingly common in hot-climate jurisdictions. Combined with insulation upgrades for maximum efficiency.

plain: A low-risk Real Estate investment strategy targeting stabilised, top-quality property — modest leverage, steady cash flow, single-digit IRR targets.
snappy: Lowest-risk Real Estate strategy — stabilised Class A property, modest leverage, single-digit IRR.
detail: Core sits at the low-risk end of the Real Estate strategy spectrum, alongside Core-Plus (slightly higher risk), Value-Add (moderate-risk Rehab), and Opportunistic (highest-risk development or distressed). Core deals target stabilised Class A property in major markets, leverage at 40-55% LTV, Hold Period 7-10+ years, IRR 7-10% (unlevered) or 8-12% (levered), with most of the return from cash yield rather than appreciation. Pension funds, sovereign wealth, and listed REITs dominate Core capital. Cap Rate Compression hit hardest in Core during 2015-2022.

plain: A Real Estate investment strategy one step riskier than Core — stabilised property with slightly more leverage, value-add potential, or secondary markets.
snappy: Real Estate strategy between Core and Value-Add — stabilised property, moderate leverage.
detail: Core-Plus deals target stabilised property in good condition that has light improvement potential — minor renovation, modest Rent-roll mark-to-market, modest Cap-Ex. Leverage runs 55-65% LTV (above Core's 40-55%). Hold Period 5-10 years. Levered IRR target 10-13%, mostly from cash flow with modest appreciation. Common Core-Plus moves: lease-up a 90% leased Office to 95%, renovate Multifamily Common Areas without unit interiors, rebrand a Hotel. Less risk than Value-Add (no major Rehab or repositioning), more upside than Core.

plain: A smaller bank or Mortgage company that originates and closes loans in its own name — then sells them to a larger 'sponsor' bank shortly after Closing.
snappy: Smaller Lender originating Mortgages in own name, then selling to a sponsor bank post-close.
detail: Correspondent lending is the middle path between Mortgage Banker (holds or sells to GSEs directly) and Mortgage Broker (never funds). The correspondent funds the loan using its own warehouse line, then sells closed loans to a sponsor bank (Wells Fargo, Chase, US Bank, PennyMac) within days or weeks. The sponsor reunderwrites, repurchases unacceptable loans, and either holds or sells onward. Correspondent Lenders gain pricing scale they couldn't reach independently while keeping the relationship with the borrower. Community banks and credit unions often run correspondent operations to keep mortgage operations profitable.

plain: An Appraisal method that values a property as the cost to rebuild it from scratch, minus Depreciation for age and wear, plus Land value.
snappy: Appraisal method valuing improvements at replacement cost less Depreciation plus Land value.
detail: The cost approach works best for new or special-use property: a school, fire station, brand-new build, or unique property with no Comps. The Appraiser estimates the cost to construct an equivalent building today (Replacement Cost) or to reproduce the exact building (reproduction cost), subtracts accrued Depreciation (physical wear, Functional Obsolescence, External Obsolescence), and adds the Land's value to reach total value. For old, conventional property the cost approach is least reliable — accrued Depreciation estimates carry too much error.

plain: What you paid for a property — plus capital improvements, minus Depreciation — that determines Capital Gain on Sale.
snappy: Purchase price plus improvements minus Depreciation — the basis for Capital Gain calculation.
detail: Cost basis is the tax accounting record of what the owner has invested in the property. Start with: purchase price + acquisition costs (title fees, transfer tax, attorney). Add: capital improvements (kitchen renovation, new Roof, additions — not routine repairs). Subtract: Depreciation taken (for investment property). On Sale, gain = Sale Price − Cost Basis − selling costs. Errors are common. Long-held investment property accumulates major Depreciation that reduces basis below the original purchase price. Step-up in Basis at death resets basis to fair market value.

plain: A tax study that accelerates Depreciation deductions on a building by reclassifying parts of it as shorter-life assets.
snappy: Engineering study accelerating Depreciation on commercial property assets.
detail: A cost-segregation study breaks a building's purchase price into components with different IRS Depreciation lives — the building shell stays at 27.5 (residential) or 39 (commercial) years, but carpets, fixtures, parking lot, and landscaping qualify for 5-, 7-, or 15-year schedules. Front-loading Depreciation boosts after-tax cash flow in the early years of ownership. Most useful for buildings over $500K. Recapture at sale claws some benefit back.

plain: A formal engineering-based analysis of a commercial property's components — identifying personal-property elements that qualify for 5, 7, or 15-year Depreciation versus 27.5/39-year Real Property.
snappy: Engineering study identifying property components qualifying for accelerated Depreciation.
detail: Cost Segregation Studies separate Personal Property and land improvements (5, 7, 15-year MACRS) from building shell (27.5 or 39-year). Eligible items: carpet, cabinets, decorative lighting, parking lot striping, landscaping, water features, signage. Typical reclassification: 20-30% of acquisition cost shifts to shorter MACRS lives. Bonus Depreciation amplifies this. Cost: $5,000-$20,000 for the study, paying for itself many times over through accelerated tax deductions.

plain: A seller's modified response to a buyer's offer — usually a different price or terms.
snappy: Modified response to an offer that becomes a new offer requiring acceptance.
detail: A counteroffer legally rejects the original offer and substitutes new terms — the original is dead. The party who counter-offers becomes the new offeror; the other party must accept, counter again, or walk. Counters typically adjust price, Closing date, Contingency timing, or specific concessions like seller-paid Closing Costs. Sophisticated negotiations often involve three or four rounds of counters before signing.

plain: A binding promise written into a Deed or HOA rules — about how the property can be used.
snappy: Recorded promise restricting how a property is used; runs with the land.
detail: Covenants run with the land — every successor owner is bound regardless of whether they were a party to the original agreement. CC&Rs are the most common bundle of covenants in residential subdivisions and condo communities. Older Deeds occasionally contain racially restrictive covenants — these have been federally unenforceable since the 1948 Supreme Court ruling in Shelley v. Kraemer but often survive on paper as historical artefacts.

plain: A shared Office Tenant model — multiple companies and freelancers share a single workspace under flexible memberships — pioneered by WeWork, Regus, Industrious.
snappy: Shared Office Tenant model — multiple companies share workspace under flexible memberships.
detail: Coworking emerged in the 2000s and accelerated 2010-2020 before WeWork's collapse and post-2020 hybrid-work disruption. Models: dedicated desks (assigned), hot desks (rotating), private offices within shared facility, virtual office (mailing address + occasional access). Members: freelancers, small startups, satellite teams of larger companies, project teams. Major operators: Regus (oldest, largest), WeWork (peaked 2019), Industrious, Spaces, Convene, Workspring. Cap Rate impact: Coworking-anchored Office buildings face Tenant-concentration risk; primary Tenant credit-quality drops; some institutional Lenders restrict Coworking exposure.

plain: The federal law requiring banks to meet credit needs in all communities they serve — driving lending into low-income and minority neighbourhoods.
snappy: Federal law requiring banks to lend in all communities, including low-income neighbourhoods.
detail: CRA was enacted 1977 to combat Redlining. Federal banking regulators (OCC, FDIC, Federal Reserve) examine each bank's lending and rate it Outstanding, Satisfactory, Needs to Improve, or Substantial Non-Compliance. Below-Satisfactory ratings block mergers and branch openings. CRA-driven activity: small-business lending, LIHTC investment, community-development lending. Banks contribute hundreds of billions in housing-related capital annually under CRA pressure. The 2023 CRA reform updated assessment framework.

plain: Common shorthand for Commercial Real Estate — income-producing investment property like Office, Retail, Industrial, Multifamily, and Hotel.
snappy: Standard shorthand for Commercial Real Estate in investment circles.
detail: CRE is universal industry shorthand for Commercial Real Estate. Practitioners use 'CRE deals', 'CRE finance', 'CRE Cap Rates' constantly. See Commercial Real Estate for the substantive coverage of asset classes, return characteristics, and how CRE differs from residential ownership.

plain: A three-digit summary of how reliably you've repaid debt — Lenders use it to price your Mortgage.
snappy: Numeric credit-risk score; FICO 300-850 is the dominant US scale.
detail: Mortgage Lenders use FICO scores from all three credit bureaus and typically take the middle score. Conventional Loans usually require 620+; FHA Loans go as low as 580 (or 500 with 10% Down Payment); VA and USDA have no hard minimum but Lenders impose their own (often 620). Higher scores access lower interest rates and lower PMI. A 100-point score difference can mean tens of thousands in lifetime interest.

plain: A loan structure where multiple properties secure a single loan — or multiple loans share a single collateral pool — concentrating Lender protection across the portfolio.
snappy: Loan structure where multiple properties secure a single loan, or vice versa.
detail: Cross-Collateralization gives Lenders broader recovery options. A Sponsor with three Multifamily properties might cross-collateralise them under a single $50M Mortgage — Default on the loan can trigger Foreclosure on all three properties. Alternatively, three separate loans (one per property) might cross-collateralise where Default on any one allows Foreclosure on all. Pros for Lender: broader collateral, harder for Sponsor to 'cherry-pick' good versus bad assets in distress. Cons for Sponsor: loss of optionality, inability to sell or refinance individual properties without releasing them from the cross-collateral structure. Release provisions in loan documents specify the conditions and pricing.

plain: A loan provision that treats Default on one loan as automatic Default on another related loan — typically across multiple loans to the same borrower or sponsor.
snappy: Loan provision treating Default on one loan as automatic Default on another related loan.
detail: Cross-Default provisions amplify Default consequences for borrowers with multiple Loans from the same Lender (or to the same Sponsor). Mechanics: Default on any one cross-defaulted Loan triggers Default on all linked Loans, often regardless of payment status on the others. Lenders use Cross-Default to prevent Sponsors from selectively defaulting on one Loan to preserve equity in others. Sponsors prefer ring-fencing — each property in a separate single-purpose entity with no Cross-Default to other holdings. Negotiation: large Sponsors often achieve full ring-fencing; smaller Sponsors face Cross-Default in their first deals as part of relationship-building with Lenders.

plain: An Industrial building configured for through-flow logistics — inbound trucks on one side, outbound trucks on the other — minimising on-site storage.
snappy: Industrial building with through-flow logistics, dock doors on both sides.
detail: Cross-Dock facilities trade storage for throughput. Configuration: dock doors on opposing long sides of the building, allowing inbound trailers to unload at one end and outbound to load at the other within hours, never inventorying in racking. Common Tenants: parcel carriers (FedEx, UPS), grocery distribution, retail consolidation. Building dimensions: typically 200-400 feet wide and 800-1,500 feet long, with 1:1 inbound-outbound dock door ratio. Truck Court depth is critical on both sides. Cross-Dock requires more land per square foot of building than conventional warehouse; suitable parcels are scarce in dense urban infill markets.

plain: How attractive a property looks from the street — paint, landscaping, front door — strongly affects sale price.
snappy: First-impression visual appeal of a property from the street.
detail: Curb Appeal is the first signal buyers form about a property before stepping inside. Sellers invest in landscaping, exterior paint, front-door refresh, and tidy walkways to boost it before listing. Empirical studies suggest strong curb appeal lifts sale price 5-7% versus identical homes with poor exteriors. Agents almost universally recommend curb-appeal work as the highest-ROI pre-listing investment.

plain: A house built to the buyer's specific design and specifications — architect-drawn plans, custom finishes, longer build time, premium price.
snappy: House built to buyer-specific design with custom finishes and floor plan.
detail: Custom homes start with an architect (or buyer-purchased plans) and a Lot the buyer typically owns. The builder works on cost-plus, GMP, or stipulated-sum contracts. Timelines: 12-24 months from breaking ground for a true custom build. Cost premium over comparable tract: 30-100%, depending on market and finish level. Common reasons buyers go custom: specific Lot constraints (slope, view, water access), specific design preferences (architectural style, layout), or specific finish quality (high-end mechanical, premium materials). Cost overrun risk is the buyer's primary friction — change orders are expensive.

plain: Insurance covering corporate executives — REIT directors, syndication GP officers, Condo board members, HOA board members — against personal liability for board decisions.
snappy: Insurance covering executives against personal liability for board decisions.
detail: D&O coverage protects corporate decision-makers from personal liability. Real Estate scenarios: HOA boards sued over CAM decisions, Condo boards sued over Special Assessment imposition, REIT directors sued over Sale or acquisition decisions, syndication GP officers sued over fiduciary breach. Limits: $1M-$10M+. Personal-attribution exclusions apply — fraud, criminal acts, intentional misconduct. Side-A coverage protects officers when corporate indemnification is unavailable.

plain: Specialised Commercial buildings housing computer servers and IT infrastructure — high power consumption, advanced cooling, fibre connectivity, security — most-grown asset class of 2020s.
snappy: Specialised Commercial buildings housing servers and IT infrastructure.
detail: Data Centers became a dominant institutional Real Estate asset class with cloud computing growth. Building specs: extreme power density (30-100+ MW per facility), N+1 or 2N redundancy on power and cooling, robust generator backup, security clearance protocols, fibre connectivity to multiple providers. Tenants: hyperscale cloud (AWS, Azure, Google), telecom carriers, large enterprise IT. Cap Rates: 4-5.5% for stabilised facilities. Major Data Center REITs: Equinix (largest, $90B+ market cap), Digital Realty, CyrusOne (private since 2022). Hyperscale customers increasingly Build-to-Suit lease arrangements.

plain: How long a property has been listed for sale — a key signal of pricing and demand.
snappy: Calendar days since a property hit the market.
detail: DOM tracks calendar days from MLS listing date to contract acceptance. Hot markets see medians under 7 days; slow markets stretch to 60-90+. Days on Market is one of the most-watched market-temperature signals — alongside list-to-sale ratio and inventory months supply. Re-listing tricks (cancel and relist to reset DOM) are widely used and partially defeated by MLS rules tracking cumulative DOM across re-listings.

plain: Common shorthand for Discounted Cash Flow — the valuation method projecting future cash flows and discounting them back to present value.
snappy: Standard shorthand for Discounted Cash Flow in valuation.
detail: DCF is universal industry shorthand for Discounted Cash Flow analysis. Real Estate analysts and institutional investors cite 'the DCF' as shorthand for the underwriting model itself. See Discounted Cash Flow for the methodology, sensitivities to Exit Cap Rate and discount rate, and how DCF compares to direct capitalisation as a valuation approach for stabilised property.

plain: A Lender's stress metric — NOI divided by loan amount — gauging the property's ability to service debt even under pessimistic Cap Rate scenarios.
snappy: NOI divided by loan amount — Lender's stress metric for debt-coverage at varying Cap Rates.
detail: Debt Yield is the Lender-side alternative to LTV. Calculation: NOI ÷ loan amount. A property with $1M NOI and an $8M loan has 12.5% debt yield. Debt Yield is insensitive to Cap Rate movements — unlike LTV which depends on Sale Price. Conservative Commercial Lenders require minimum debt yields: 8-9% Multifamily, 9-10% Office, 10-11% Retail, 11-12% Hotel. The metric drove post-2008 CMBS Underwriting reform — pre-crisis Lenders priced almost entirely on LTV and DSCR, missing that Cap Rate Compression had pushed property values artificially high. Debt Yield rose to prominence as the structural-floor metric in commercial mortgage analysis.

plain: The full spelling of DTI — the monthly-debt-to-monthly-income ratio Lenders use to size a Mortgage.
snappy: Full spelling of DTI — the borrower's debt-to-income ratio.
detail: Debt-to-Income Ratio is the formal spelling of DTI, the headline qualification metric for residential Mortgage underwriting. Two flavours: front-end (housing-only, typically capped 28%) and back-end (all debt, typically capped 36-45% depending on program). Higher ratios may clear with compensating factors — reserves, a high Credit Score, or a large Down Payment. See DTI for the operational mechanics; this entry exists so prose written out longhand also auto-links.

plain: The legal document that transfers ownership of a property from seller to buyer — signed at Closing and filed with the county.
snappy: Written instrument conveying real-property Title between parties.
detail: A deed transfers ownership from grantor to grantee. The instrument must be written, identify the parties and property, contain words of conveyance, and be signed by the grantor. Common types: warranty deed (full Title guarantees), special warranty deed (limited guarantees), Quitclaim Deed (no guarantees — common in divorce or family transfers), and Deed of Trust (used in place of a Mortgage in many states). Deeds must be recorded with the county to give public notice.

plain: When a struggling borrower hands the property back to the Lender voluntarily instead of going through Foreclosure.
snappy: Voluntary transfer of Deed to Lender to avoid Foreclosure.
detail: A deed in lieu is a workout: rather than fight the Foreclosure process, the borrower deeds the property directly to the Lender in exchange for cancellation of the Mortgage debt. Faster and cheaper than Foreclosure for both sides, and less damaging to the borrower's Credit Score. The Lender must accept — they may refuse if junior Liens or other encumbrances complicate Title. Tax: forgiven debt can be taxable income, though some federal exclusions apply.

plain: An alternative to a Mortgage used in many US states — a third party (trustee) holds Title until the loan is paid.
snappy: Three-party security instrument with a trustee holding Title until payoff.
detail: States divide between Mortgage states and Deed of Trust states. In a Deed of Trust state (California, Texas, Virginia, and most of the West), the borrower conveys Title to a trustee who holds it for the Lender. On Default, the trustee can foreclose non-judicially — faster and cheaper than the judicial Foreclosure required in Mortgage states. Functionally equivalent to a Mortgage from the borrower's perspective.

plain: Failing to keep up with Mortgage payments or otherwise breaching the loan agreement.
snappy: Breach of the Mortgage contract, usually missed payments.
detail: Default is the breach that triggers the Acceleration Clause and ultimately Foreclosure. Most Mortgages enter technical default after 30 days late and serious default after 90. Lenders generally try to work with borrowers (forbearance, loan modification, short sale) before foreclosing because foreclosure is costly and produces a discounted REO sale. Loan loss provisioning and CMBS investor reporting use specific 60+ and 90+ day default metrics.

plain: The process of pre-paying a CMBS or other locked Commercial loan by substituting US Treasuries for the property as collateral — expensive, formulaic, the dominant exit when Sale or refinance is needed mid-Lease.
snappy: Pre-paying a CMBS loan by substituting Treasuries for the property as collateral.
detail: Defeasance was invented for CMBS to allow pre-payment without disturbing bond cash flows. Mechanics: the borrower purchases a portfolio of US Treasuries that generates exactly the Mortgage's remaining payment schedule. The Treasuries get substituted into the Mortgage's collateral; the borrower's property is released. Cost depends on rate environment: lower rates today than at origination push defeasance cost up (Treasuries cost more to generate the same cash flow); higher rates push cost down. Defeasance professionals (Chatham Financial, Commercial Defeasance LLC) shop the Treasury market and structure the transaction. Costs: $200,000-$500,000+ in fees and rate differential.

plain: A Zoning incentive letting a developer build more units than the base allowance — in exchange for providing Affordable Housing, open space, or other public benefits.
snappy: Zoning incentive allowing extra density in exchange for public benefits.
detail: California's Density Bonus Law (Government Code §65915) is the national prototype: a developer who provides 10% of units as Affordable Housing earns up to 35% additional units; deeper affordability earns more. Local jurisdictions implement variations — TDR (transfer of development rights), historic-preservation bonuses, transit-oriented bonuses, green-building bonuses.
