Density Bonus is the developer's lever to make Affordable Housing economically feasible — the additional market-rate units cross-subsidise the discounted ones. Critical to LIHTC layered deals where Density Bonus is essential to viability.

plain: The yearly tax deduction investors take to reflect that a building wears out — even though most rise in market value.
snappy: Annual tax deduction for the wear-and-tear of an income property.
detail: The IRS treats every commercial building as wearing out over 39 years and every residential rental over 27.5 years (the land underneath isn't depreciable). The annual deduction reduces taxable income from rent without an actual cash expense — a major reason real-estate investment is tax-favoured. Cost Segregation accelerates the timeline by reclassifying components. Depreciation taken is recaptured at 25% federal when the property is sold, unless rolled into a 1031 Exchange.

plain: A tax claw-back at the Sale of a depreciated property — gains attributable to prior Depreciation deductions are taxed at a higher rate than long-term Capital Gain.
snappy: Tax claw-back at sale on gain previously deducted as Depreciation, at elevated rates.
detail: When a depreciated property sells, IRS recharacterises a portion of the gain as ordinary depreciation recapture rather than long-term Capital Gain. For Real Property under §1250, the recapture rate is capped at 25%. For personal-property components (carpeting, appliances, parking lot improvements identified through Cost Segregation) under §1245, recapture is at full ordinary rates — up to 37%. 1031 Exchange defers depreciation recapture along with Capital Gain. Step-up in Basis at death eliminates both.

plain: When buyer and seller use different Agents inside the same brokerage — the alternative to Dual Agency.
snappy: Separate Agents inside one brokerage representing buyer and seller.
detail: Designated Agency lets two Agents in the same brokerage represent opposing parties in a single transaction. Each owes fiduciary duty to their client; the Broker walks a neutral line above them. Adopted in many states as a less-conflicted alternative to Dual Agency. Critics argue Broker-level loyalty conflicts persist; defenders argue agent-level separation provides meaningful client advocacy. Real estate Commission economics typically remain unchanged from a single-brokerage transaction.

plain: Special Loan financing extended to a company in Chapter 11 bankruptcy — has Super-Senior priority over pre-petition Lenders, letting the company continue operating during reorganisation.
snappy: Bankruptcy financing with Super-Senior priority over pre-petition Lenders.
detail: DIP Financing keeps Chapter 11 debtors operational during reorganisation. Pre-petition Lenders typically agree to subordinate to DIP debt (or themselves provide DIP financing). Pricing: substantially above-market — typical DIP rates 10-15% in 2024 — given the borrower's distressed state. Court approval required for DIP Financing terms. Common in: hotel Chapter 11s (during 2020), retail Chapter 11s, large commercial workouts. DIP Lenders monitor borrower operations closely; reorganisation plans typically convert DIP into exit financing.

plain: A simple valuation method: take a property's NOI for one year and divide by the market Cap Rate to get value.
snappy: Valuation method dividing one year's NOI by market Cap Rate to derive value.
detail: Direct capitalisation is the everyday Real Estate valuation shortcut. NOI ÷ Cap Rate = Value. A property generating $1M NOI in a 5% Cap Rate market values at $20M. Strengths: simple, requires only one year of NOI and a market Cap Rate. Weaknesses: ignores variable cash flow over time, doesn't model Cap-Ex cycles or refinance, assumes the market Cap Rate is correctly observed. The Income Approach uses direct capitalisation for stabilised properties and Discounted Cash Flow for properties with variable cash flow or value-add business plans.

plain: Written information the seller must give the buyer about known defects, hazards, or material facts.
snappy: Seller's required written statement of known property issues.
detail: Most US states require sellers to fill out a disclosure form covering known issues — roof leaks, foundation cracks, mould, neighbour disputes, pending litigation, lead paint (mandatory federal disclosure for pre-1978 homes), and similar. The standard is what the seller actually knew, not what they should have noticed. Buyers who later discover an undisclosed material defect can sue for damages. Inspector findings supplement disclosure but don't replace it.

plain: Upfront fees you pay the Lender at Closing to permanently lower your Mortgage's interest rate.
snappy: Prepaid Interest fee at Closing, each point ~1% of loan size for ~0.25% rate cut.
detail: One discount point equals 1% of the loan amount and typically reduces the interest rate by 0.25%, though the exact ratio varies by Lender and market. Points are a form of Buy-Down: paying for a lower rate over the life of the loan. The break-even depends on how long the borrower keeps the Mortgage — generally 5-7 years to recover the upfront cost via lower monthly Interest. Disclosed on the Loan Estimate and rolled into APR.

plain: The annual rate used to convert future cash flows to present value in a Discounted Cash Flow valuation — typically the investor's target return.
snappy: Annual rate used to discount future cash flows to present value in DCF.
detail: The Discount Rate in Real Estate DCF is the investor's required return given the deal's risk profile. Conventions: unlevered Discount Rate for property-level analysis (no debt), levered for equity-level. Components: risk-free rate (typically 10-year Treasury) + Real Estate equity risk premium (3-5%) + property-specific risk (asset class, location, business plan). Typical 2024 unlevered Discount Rates: 7-9% Core Multifamily, 8-10% Value-Add Office, 9-12% Opportunistic Industrial. NPV is most sensitive to Discount Rate; small changes shift terminal value substantially.

plain: A valuation method that projects every year's cash flow and the exit Sale Price, then discounts them back to present value using a target return rate.
snappy: Valuation method discounting projected cash flows back to present value at a target rate.
detail: DCF dominates institutional Commercial Real Estate underwriting. The model projects 5-10 years of annual NOI (after Cap-Ex and Replacement Reserve), an Exit Cap Rate applied to year-N+1 NOI for reversion value, and discounts every cash flow back at a target unlevered return (often 7-12% depending on risk). The IRR that makes NPV equal zero is the deal's projected return. DCF is more sensitive than direct capitalisation to: Rent growth assumptions, Exit Cap Rate, discount rate. Sensitivity tables surround the base case. The Income Approach uses DCF as its primary methodology for stabilised property.

plain: A Sponsor fee charged to LPs at the Sale of a property — typically 1-2% of Sale Price — paid at closing of the disposition.
snappy: Sponsor fee at the Sale of a property — 1-2% of Sale Price.
detail: Disposition Fees pay the Sponsor for managing the Sale process — selecting brokers, marketing the property, evaluating offers, negotiating, navigating Due Diligence, and Closing. Range: 0.5-2.0% of Sale Price. Some institutional Sponsors waive or reduce disposition fees when commission to a broker is already substantial. Aggressive Sponsors charge disposition fees on top of broker commissions plus acquisition fees on the next deal — a 'churn' pattern LPs flag. Disposition Fees come off the top of Sale proceeds, reducing the cash available to investors and Promote. Institutional LP terms often limit or eliminate disposition fees in favour of higher Sponsor Promote alignment.

plain: A property whose owner can no longer service the debt or operate it profitably — opportunities for buyers with capital and patience to acquire below replacement cost.
snappy: Property whose owner can't service debt or operate profitably — discount buying opportunity.
detail: Distressed assets surface in down cycles. Causes: maturity defaults (loan comes due in a high-rate environment, can't refinance), operating shortfalls (vacancy, declining Rents), sponsor mismanagement, structural obsolescence. The acquisition path varies. Direct purchase from the owner at distressed pricing. Note acquisition from the Lender (buy the Mortgage, then negotiate with the borrower or foreclose). Foreclosure auction. Deed in Lieu negotiations. REO purchases after Foreclosure. Distressed cycles (1990 Resolution Trust, 2008-2012, 2023-2024 office) generate the largest one-time Real Estate fortunes — and the largest losses for sellers.

plain: A Mortgage trading below face value — the borrower's distress or the property's value collapse pushes the loan's market price down, attracting opportunistic buyers.
snappy: Mortgage trading below face value due to borrower distress or property collapse.
detail: Distressed Debt investing in Real Estate revives in cycles: 1990 RTC, 2008-2012, 2023-2024 office. Investors buy the loan from the Lender (or Special Servicer in CMBS) at 40-70 cents on the dollar of face value, then pursue one of several exit paths: (1) Workout — renegotiate terms with the borrower, expecting partial loss but retention of cash-flowing asset. (2) Loan-to-Own — drive the borrower into Default and Foreclosure, taking the property at the loan's discounted basis. (3) Discounted payoff — borrower pays less than face but more than the investor's purchase price. Outcomes hinge on property quality, Sponsor cooperation, and special-servicer behaviour.

plain: Common shorthand for the Dodd-Frank Act — the 2010 financial-reform law that reshaped Mortgage lending.
snappy: Standard shorthand for the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform Act.
detail: Dodd-Frank is the industry shorthand for the Dodd-Frank Act, named after Senator Chris Dodd and Representative Barney Frank. The shorthand dominates day-to-day conversation in Mortgage compliance and consumer-finance circles. See Dodd-Frank Act for the substantive mortgage-lending provisions: CFPB creation, Qualified Mortgage rules, ability-to-repay, Loan Officer compensation restrictions.

full: Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act
plain: The 2010 financial-reform law that created the CFPB and overhauled Mortgage lending rules after the 2008 crisis.
snappy: 2010 financial-reform statute creating the CFPB and rewriting mortgage origination rules.
detail: Dodd-Frank tightened residential Mortgage lending after the 2008 collapse. Created the CFPB and gave it rule-writing authority. Imposed the ability-to-repay rule and the Qualified Mortgage safe harbour (DTI cap, no risky features). Restricted Loan Officer compensation to prevent steering. Created mandatory escrows for higher-priced loans. Imposed risk-retention on private MBS issuers. The statute is sprawling; most retail-side impact for Real Estate flows through CFPB regulations (TRID, Reg Z, Reg X).

plain: A commercial Lease where the Tenant pays Property Tax and insurance — but not maintenance — in addition to Base Rent.
snappy: Commercial Lease where Tenant pays Property Tax and insurance, but not maintenance.
detail: Double Net Lease (NN Lease) is the middle Net Lease tier. The Tenant absorbs Property Tax and insurance variability while the Landlord remains responsible for maintenance, repairs, and Cap-Ex. Common in older Commercial Real Estate transactions, some Industrial, and some Office. The Tenant shoulders inflation-sensitive line items (Property Tax growth, insurance market cycles) but doesn't take on structural maintenance risk. NN survives most often in inherited Leases — newer deals more commonly use NNN (Triple Net Lease) for clearer Landlord/Tenant cost separation. Specific NN allocations are heavily negotiated in renewal cycles.

plain: The cash you put down upfront when buying a home — the rest is the Mortgage.
snappy: Cash paid by the buyer at Closing, with the Lender financing the balance.
detail: Conventional Loans typically require 5-20% down; FHA Loans allow 3.5% with mortgage insurance; VA Loans and USDA Loans permit zero down for eligible borrowers. A 20% Down Payment lets Conventional borrowers avoid PMI and often unlocks better pricing tiers. Down Payment combined with LTV defines the borrower's initial Equity. Larger down payments increase loan approval odds and reduce interest rate.

plain: Government or non-profit programs helping first-time homebuyers cover the Down Payment — grants, forgivable Loans, or matched savings.
snappy: Programs helping first-time homebuyers cover Down Payment via grants or forgivable Loans.
detail: Down Payment Assistance (DPA) programs operate at federal, state, and local levels. Forgivable loans: $5,000-$50,000+ that forgive over 5-10 years if borrower stays in home. Grants: outright Down Payment cash, no repayment. Matched-savings programs (Individual Development Accounts): government matches savings dollar-for-dollar up to a limit. State housing finance agencies (CalHFA, NYS HCR, Texas HFA) operate the largest programs. Eligibility: typically First-Time Homebuyer, income below 80-120% of Area Median Income, occupancy requirements. Major programs: CalHFA MyHome Assistance Program, Florida Hometown Heroes, NY SONYMA Programs.

plain: Aerial property photos and video — captured by FAA-certified drone operators — showing properties from elevated angles for marketing and surveying.
snappy: Aerial photos and video of property captured by FAA-certified drone operators.
detail: Drone Photography has become standard listing marketing for higher-tier properties. Uses: aerial property photos showcasing Lot size and surroundings, neighbourhood orientation, video flythrough, roof and exterior inspection, agricultural Land documentation. FAA requires Part 107 commercial operator certification for paid drone work. Privacy concerns: neighbour complaints about drone flights over adjacent property; some HOAs and municipalities restrict drone use. Cost: $200-$1,500 for residential Drone Photography. Real Estate consistently among the largest commercial drone-use sectors.

plain: For investment properties — how many times the rental income covers the Mortgage payment.
snappy: NOI divided by annual debt service — coverage cushion on a commercial loan.
detail: DSCR is the commercial real estate analogue of Debt-to-Income Ratio. NOI divided by annual debt service: 1.20 means the property generates 20% more income than required to cover the Mortgage. Most commercial Lenders require 1.20-1.25 minimum at Underwriting. DSCR loans for single-family rentals exploded post-2020 — they qualify the borrower based on the property's rent rather than personal income.

plain: A loan term requiring the borrower to maintain a minimum DSCR — typically 1.20x or 1.25x — throughout the loan term, with cures or Defaults for shortfalls.
snappy: Loan covenant requiring minimum DSCR throughout the loan term.
detail: DSCR Covenants are core Commercial Mortgage protections for Lenders. Typical: minimum 1.20x DSCR measured quarterly or annually. Below-covenant DSCR triggers: cash sweeping (excess cash flow held in Lender escrow rather than distributed to equity), cure options (sponsor injection to bring DSCR back above threshold), partial recourse, or technical Default. Loan documents typically include a 'springing cash management' provision: at the moment DSCR falls below covenant, all property cash flows route through Lender-controlled accounts. Sponsors carefully model DSCR through downside scenarios; covenant Defaults during 2020-2021 hospitality and 2023-2024 office cycles triggered widespread workout activity.

plain: Your monthly debt payments divided by your monthly income — Lenders cap how high it can go to qualify.
snappy: Monthly debt obligations divided by gross monthly income.
detail: Lenders compute two DTIs: front-end (Mortgage payment, Property Tax, insurance, HOA divided by income) and back-end (all of the above plus car loans, student loans, minimum credit card payments). Most Conforming Loans cap back-end DTI at 43-45%, though Conventional Loan AUS approvals stretch to 50%. DTI is the single biggest determinant of Mortgage qualification alongside Credit Score.

plain: When one agent or brokerage represents both the buyer and the seller in the same transaction.
snappy: Single agent or Broker representing both buyer and seller in one deal.
detail: Dual Agency creates an inherent conflict — the agent owes fiduciary duties to both sides simultaneously. Some states ban it outright; others allow it with written disclosure and informed consent. Critics argue it incentivises closing the deal over advocating for either party. A variant — designated agency — assigns different agents within the same brokerage to each side, narrowing the conflict to the Broker level.

plain: The investigation period after going under contract — inspections, document review, surveys — before the deal closes.
snappy: Investigation period during which the buyer verifies the property and its records.
detail: In residential transactions, due diligence runs through the Contingency periods — typically 7-14 days for inspection, 14-21 for Appraisal. The buyer hires professionals (Inspector, Appraiser, surveyor) and reviews documents (HOA financials, CC&Rs, Title Insurance commitment, lead-paint disclosure). Commercial due diligence is longer (30-90 days) and broader: phase I environmental, tenant interviews, lease audit, market study. Findings drive renegotiation or termination via Contingency.

full: Errors and Omissions Insurance, Professional Liability
plain: Insurance covering Real Estate professionals — Agents, brokers, appraisers, property managers — against claims of negligence, errors, or breach of fiduciary duty.
snappy: Insurance covering Real Estate professionals against negligence and breach of duty claims.
detail: E&O Insurance is mandatory for licensed Real Estate Agents and brokers in nearly every US state. Coverage: claims from clients alleging negligent advice, failure to disclose material facts, misrepresentation of property condition. Typical limits: $500,000-$1M per claim. Premiums: $500-$2,000 annually for Agents. Common claims drivers: undisclosed defects, dual-agency conflicts, contract drafting errors, missed deadlines. The post-Burnett era has expanded litigation exposure.

plain: Cash you put down with your offer to show the seller you're serious — applied to the purchase if the deal closes.
snappy: Good-faith deposit accompanying a purchase offer; credited at Closing.
detail: Earnest Money signals commitment. Typically 1-3% of price in normal markets, 5-10% in competitive ones. EMD is held in Escrow by the Broker, attorney, or title company. If the buyer terminates within Contingency periods (inspection, Appraisal, financing), the EMD is refunded. Walking away after Contingencies expire generally forfeits the EMD to the seller as liquidated damages.

plain: An optional addition to Homeowners Insurance covering earthquake damage — typically with high deductibles (10-25% of dwelling value) and limited coverage scope.
snappy: Optional Homeowners Insurance addition for earthquake damage — high deductibles, limited scope.
detail: Earthquake Endorsements supplement standard Homeowners Insurance which excludes earthquake. Deductibles: 10-25% of dwelling coverage value — much higher than standard policy deductibles. Coverage scope: dwelling damage only, some endorsements include contents; loss-of-use coverage variable. Premium: $1,500-$5,000+/year in California, less in moderate-risk states (Washington, Oregon, Utah, Missouri). Most Homeowners decline EQ Endorsements due to cost. California Earthquake Authority dominates that state's EQ market; private endorsements available in lower-risk states. Mortgage Lenders typically don't require EQ Endorsements.

plain: Insurance covering damage from earthquake events — separate from Homeowners Insurance, mostly provided through the California Earthquake Authority in California or as private endorsements elsewhere.
snappy: Separate insurance covering earthquake damage — not included in standard Homeowners Insurance.
detail: Homeowners Insurance excludes earthquake damage. California (most exposed state) created the California Earthquake Authority (CEA, 1996) — a state-run pool that writes most California EQ policies, with premiums tied to building age, construction type, and seismic zone. Coverage is high-deductible (often 10-25% of dwelling value) and expensive ($1,500-$5,000+/year for typical homes). Other West Coast states use private carriers exclusively. Adoption rates are low — ~10-15% of California homeowners carry EQ — because of cost and deductible structure. Commercial property in seismic zones almost always carries Earthquake Insurance; high-rise tower co-ops often require it.

plain: A right to use part of someone else's Land for a specific purpose — like a shared driveway or a utility line.
snappy: Limited right to use another party's Real Property for a defined purpose.
detail: Easements run with the Land — they bind future owners, not just the current one. Common types: utility easements (power, water, sewer), access easements (driveways crossing a neighbour's Lot), conservation easements (restricting development). Created by Deed, prescription (long use, like Adverse Possession), or necessity (landlocked parcels). Title Insurance and Inspections should surface recorded easements; unrecorded prescriptive easements are a litigation risk. A holder who oversteps the scope becomes a trespasser.

plain: An Easement that benefits one specific Lot — the dominant estate — and is recorded against another Lot — the servient estate — running with the Land for both.
snappy: Easement benefiting one Lot (dominant) and burdening another (servient) — runs with the Land.
detail: Easement Appurtenant attaches to two parcels — a dominant estate (the benefited Lot) and a servient estate (the burdened Lot). Both transfer automatically with the respective Lots. Common examples: shared driveway easement where Lot A has the right to use a driveway crossing Lot B; utility easement where the city has the right to access a strip of every Lot for water and sewer. Easement Appurtenant cannot be transferred separately from its dominant estate — selling just the easement is impossible. Compare Easement in Gross: benefits a person or entity (not a Lot), can be transferred independently. Most utility and pipeline easements are easements in gross.

plain: An Easement created by law — even without a Deed — when a landlocked Lot needs access across a neighbouring parcel to reach a public road.
snappy: Law-created Easement letting a landlocked Lot reach a public road across a neighbour's Land.
detail: Easement by Necessity arises automatically when severance from a common owner creates a landlocked parcel. Example: a 100-acre tract sold off as two 50-acre parcels — the back parcel has no road frontage. Common law creates an Easement by Necessity over the front parcel even though the Deed didn't mention it. Required elements: common ownership at severance, strict necessity (not just convenience), and the necessity exists at the moment of severance. Courts apply narrowly — courts strongly prefer recorded Easements over implied ones. Sale of the landlocked parcel surfaces the Easement issue at Title search.

plain: An Easement acquired through long open use of another's Land — like Adverse Possession but creates only a right to use, not full ownership.
snappy: Easement acquired through long open use of another's Land — like Adverse Possession.
detail: Easement by Prescription arises through statutory-period use (typically 5-20 years) that is open and notorious, continuous, and adverse (without permission). The user gains a right to continue the use — typically a path or driveway across a neighbour's property — without acquiring ownership. Common scenarios: a neighbour cutting through a corner for decades, a path across a vacant Lot to reach a beach or trail. Prescriptive Easements bind successor owners. Property owners can defeat prescription by posting 'permission to cross' signs (negating adversity) or by interrupting the use briefly (resetting the clock).

plain: An Easement that benefits a person or entity — not another Lot — used by utilities, pipelines, conservation organisations to gain rights over Land without owning it.
snappy: Easement benefiting a person or entity rather than a Lot — utility lines, pipeline ROWs.
detail: Easement in Gross differs from Easement Appurtenant: there's no dominant estate, only a servient estate. The Easement holder is a person or entity. Common examples: utility company's right to maintain power lines across private property; pipeline company's right-of-way; conservation organisation's right to enforce land-use restrictions; railroad right-of-way. Easements in gross can be commercial (transferable) or personal (extinguished at the holder's death). Commercial easements in gross attach to the holder's business and pass with sale of that business — a utility's easement portfolio transfers when the utility is acquired.

plain: An entity that temporarily holds Title to a property in a Reverse 1031 Exchange — lets investors lock in replacement property before selling the relinquished one.
snappy: Entity holding Title temporarily in a Reverse 1031 Exchange.
detail: EAT is the IRS-mandated structure for Reverse 1031 Exchanges. The investor wants to buy the replacement property before selling the relinquished one. The EAT (typically a single-purpose LLC affiliated with the Qualified Intermediary) takes Title to either the replacement or the relinquished property for up to 180 days while the other side of the Exchange completes. EAT services typically cost $5,000-$15,000 beyond standard QI fees. IRS Revenue Procedure 2000-37 created the EAT safe harbour. Without an EAT, simultaneous timing requirements would make Reverse 1031 nearly impossible.

plain: The federal law banning Lender discrimination based on race, religion, sex, marital status, age, or receipt of public assistance — applies to Mortgages and all consumer credit.
snappy: Federal anti-discrimination law in lending — covers all protected classes in credit.
detail: Enacted 1974, codified at 15 USC §1691, implemented by CFPB's Regulation B. ECOA covers any extension of credit — Mortgages, auto loans, credit cards, business loans. Prohibited factors: race, colour, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age (over 18), receipt of public-assistance income, exercise of consumer-protection rights. The CFPB has brought Redlining cases under ECOA against banks for branch placement, marketing, and Underwriting that disproportionately exclude minority neighbourhoods. Adverse-action notices required when an application is denied — listing specific reasons.

plain: An Appraiser's judgment of a property's apparent age — based on condition and modernisation — rather than its calendar age.
snappy: Apparent age judged from condition and updates, distinct from chronological age.
detail: A 1950 house gutted and modernised in 2022 might have an effective age of 5 years even though chronological age is 75. Effective Age drives the Depreciation deduction in the Cost Approach. A 1990 commercial building that has been kept in showroom condition could have effective age of 15; a poorly maintained 2010 building could have effective age of 25. Appraisers reconcile effective age against the property's economic life (typical service life for the type) to estimate accrued Depreciation as a percentage.

plain: The property's actual collected Rent — Gross Rental Income minus what's lost to vacancy, concessions, and bad debt.
snappy: Gross Rental Income minus vacancy, concessions, and collection loss.
detail: EGI is the realistic top line of a property's income statement, sitting between Gross Rental Income (theoretical full-Rent at full occupancy) and NOI (after Operating Expenses). The gap between GRI and EGI shows up as the 'vacancy and collection loss' line — typically 5-10% in stabilised Multifamily, more in turnover-heavy or concession-driven markets. Sloppy underwriting confuses EGI and GRI; the latter inflates NOI by the vacancy adjustment that should sit between.

plain: Common shorthand for Effective Gross Income — Gross Rental Income minus vacancy and collection losses.
snappy: Standard shorthand for Effective Gross Income.
detail: EGI is the universal industry shorthand for Effective Gross Income. Sponsor pro formas and Lender Underwriting use 'EGI' to denote the realistic top line after vacancy and concession assumptions. See Effective Gross Income for the calculation methodology and the gap between GRI and EGI in underwriting models.

plain: The government's power to take private property for public use — paying just compensation to the owner — used for highways, schools, transit, parks.
snappy: Government power to take private property for public use with just compensation.
detail: Eminent Domain flows from the Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause — 'private property [shall not] be taken for public use, without just compensation.' Federal, state, and local governments hold the power, often delegated to public-utility companies. Common uses: highway widening, school site acquisition, transit ROW, flood-control easements. Just Compensation: fair market value as determined by Appraisal. Post-Kelo (2005) state-level reforms restricted private-purpose eminent domain in many states.

plain: When a structure or improvement crosses the property line onto a neighbour's Land — a fence, an overhanging eave, an extending driveway.
snappy: Physical intrusion of a structure or improvement onto neighbouring property.
detail: An encroachment is a survey problem with legal teeth. Even a few inches can complicate Title Insurance, frustrate Sale, or — left long enough — ripen into Adverse Possession against the original owner. Common culprits: fences built without surveys, additions extending past setbacks, roof overhangs, driveways. Discovered through a current Survey (often required by Lenders). Remedies: removal, monetary settlement, granting an Easement to legalise the encroachment, or buying the affected strip of Land.

plain: Any legal claim or restriction on a property that limits what the owner can do — a Mortgage, Lien, Easement, or use restriction.
snappy: Any third-party claim or restriction on Real Property that limits the owner's rights.
detail: Encumbrances split into financial claims (Mortgage, Lien) and use restrictions (Easement, CC&Rs, lease, Zoning overlays). Title searches and Title Insurance focus on disclosing all recorded encumbrances before Closing. Not every encumbrance kills a deal — buyers expect to take property subject to utility easements and CC&Rs. But undisclosed encumbrances (an old judgment Lien from a prior owner) are the kind of defect Title Insurance is built to cover. Sellers warrant the property free of undisclosed encumbrances in a Warranty Deed.

plain: An EPA program rating commercial buildings on energy performance — 1-100 score relative to comparable buildings — Energy Star Certified at 75+.
snappy: EPA building-energy rating — 1-100 score; Energy Star certified at 75+.
detail: Energy Star for Buildings rates whole-building energy performance using EPA's Portfolio Manager benchmarking tool. The 1-100 score reflects energy use intensity compared to similar buildings nationally. Energy Star Certified buildings score 75+ (top quartile). Major Commercial Real Estate operators publish portfolio Energy Star scores — institutional LPs and ESG-focused investors track them as proxy metrics. Many cities now require Energy Star benchmarking for buildings above size thresholds (NYC, Chicago, Philadelphia, Seattle, Washington DC). Energy Star certification renews annually; performance drift is common after initial certification.

plain: EPA's free online tool — building owners use it to track energy consumption, water use, greenhouse gas emissions across their portfolios.
snappy: EPA's free tool tracking building energy consumption across portfolios.
detail: Portfolio Manager has become essential infrastructure for Commercial Real Estate sustainability. Free EPA service; 350,000+ buildings registered. Functions: monthly utility data upload, EUI calculation, peer benchmarking, Energy Star certification application (75+ score), carbon emissions tracking, climate-resilience tools. Required by: mandatory benchmarking laws in 30+ US cities, federal buildings under Energy Act 2005, LEED certification for many credits. Pulls automatic utility data from major US utility companies via Green Button Connect. Used by virtually every institutional commercial Real Estate owner for ESG reporting and Energy Star qualification.

plain: A Mortgage that includes funds for energy-efficiency improvements — solar, insulation, HVAC upgrades — on top of the purchase or Refinance amount.
snappy: Mortgage including funds for energy-efficiency improvements beyond purchase amount.
detail: Energy-Efficient Mortgages come from multiple programs: FHA EEM, VA EEM, Conventional Energy-Improvement. Mechanics: buyer or Refinance borrower can finance up to $4,000-$8,000+ above the standard loan amount for specific energy improvements. Eligible: solar panels, insulation, HVAC efficiency, water heaters. Borrower must commission a HERS rating or RESNET audit. Improvements must show positive net present value through utility savings. EEM volume remains small but growing.

plain: The package of approvals a property has — Zoning, permits, Conditional Use, Variances — that allow specific Development to proceed.
snappy: Package of approvals giving a property the right to develop or use it in a specific way.
detail: Entitlement is the developer's primary product on raw Land. The journey: identify the Lot, propose the Zoning change or Conditional Use Permit, prepare a Site Plan, run the political process (planning commission hearings, neighbour notice, environmental review, city council vote). Successful entitlement multiplies Land value — a $5M raw site entitled for 200 apartment units may resell at $30M without any construction. Failed entitlement is the developer's biggest risk; some Sponsors specialise in entitlement as a separate business, selling shovel-ready Land to builders.

plain: Insurance covering Real Estate owners against pollution and contamination claims — historical, current, or unknown — distinct from standard CGL which excludes pollution.
snappy: Insurance covering Real Estate against pollution and contamination claims excluded from CGL.
detail: Environmental Insurance fills the pollution exclusion gap in standard CGL policies. Coverage: discovery of pre-existing contamination on owned property, third-party claims from migrating contamination, regulatory remediation costs, post-acquisition environmental liability. Common scenarios: former gas-station Lot redevelopment, dry cleaner property acquisition, industrial site purchase. Premium: highly variable, dependent on property history and current use; 0.5-3% of property value annually for high-risk sites. Major carriers: Liberty Mutual, AIG, Chubb. Brownfield redevelopment particularly depends on environmental insurance.

plain: The defaulted borrower's right — derived from common-law equity — to cure the Default and reinstate the loan at any time before Foreclosure Sale.
snappy: Borrower's common-law right to cure Default and reinstate the loan before Foreclosure Sale.
detail: Equitable Redemption is the universally-available pre-Sale cure right. Mechanics: at any time after Default and before the Foreclosure Sale, the borrower can pay the full outstanding loan balance plus accrued Interest, late fees, and Foreclosure costs — and the Lender must accept the cure, dismissing the Foreclosure. Once paid in full, the loan reinstates and the borrower keeps the property. Statutory rights sometimes augment Equitable Redemption (most state Mortgage statutes require Lenders to permit cure up until a specific time before sale). Distinct from Statutory Redemption (post-Sale repurchase right). Equitable Redemption survives every form of Foreclosure including Strict Foreclosure.

plain: What you actually own of your home — the gap between its current value and what you still owe on the Mortgage.
snappy: Owner's share — current value minus outstanding Mortgage balance.
detail: Equity equals current market value minus all outstanding debt secured against the property. A $500K home with a $300K Mortgage balance produces $200K in Equity. Equity builds two ways: Principal paydown via Amortization, and market appreciation. Owners tap Equity through cash-out Refinance, home Equity loans (a second mortgage), or HELOCs. Equity is the foundation of personal household wealth in the US — for most owners, it dwarfs other assets.

plain: How many times the investor gets their money back over the deal's life — a 2.0x equity multiple means doubling the original investment.
snappy: Total distributions divided by total invested equity over the holding period.
detail: Equity multiple is IRR's plain-English cousin. It ignores timing — a 2.0x over five years and a 2.0x over fifteen years look identical on equity multiple but very different on IRR. Both metrics get reported side-by-side in syndication offering memos. Typical Multifamily value-add targets: 1.7–2.2x equity multiple alongside 15–20% IRR. Core deals target 1.4–1.7x at 8–12% IRR. The metric is intuitive to first-time investors who get confused by IRR's compounding math.

plain: A REIT that owns and operates income-producing Real Estate — distinct from Mortgage REIT (mREIT) which lends rather than owns.
snappy: REIT owning and operating Real Estate — distinct from Mortgage REIT.
detail: Equity REITs are the dominant US REIT category — ~95% of REIT market cap. Major equity REIT subsectors: residential (Equity Residential, AvalonBay, Camden), retail (Simon, Regency, Kimco), industrial (Prologis, Duke Realty, Stag), office (Boston Properties, Vornado, SL Green), healthcare (Welltower, Ventas, Healthpeak), data centres (Equinix, Digital Realty), specialty (Public Storage, American Tower, EPR Properties). Income: 80-90% from Rent; appreciation: balance from Sale gains. Dividend yield: 3-5% typical. Listed REIT versus private/non-traded REIT distinction.

plain: A Lease provision that automatically bumps Rent up over time — fixed steps, CPI, or market-driven.
snappy: Lease provision raising Rent annually by a fixed amount, CPI, or market.
detail: Three common escalation structures. (1) Fixed steps: Rent rises a set dollar or percentage amount each year ($1/PSF, or 3%). Predictable for both parties. (2) CPI-linked: annual bumps tied to Consumer Price Index, sometimes capped. Inflation hedge for Landlord. (3) Market-based: periodic resets to market Rent, sometimes with collar/cap. Common in long-term ground leases. Multifamily Leases often skip Escalation Clauses since terms are short (12 months) and the entire Rent resets at renewal. Commercial Leases of 5-10+ years rely heavily on Escalations to grow NOI.

plain: A neutral third party that holds money or documents on behalf of the buyer and seller until the deal closes.
snappy: Third-party holding of funds or documents pending Closing.
detail: Escrow holds the Earnest Money Deposit, Closing funds, and Deed between contract and Closing — releasing each only when the conditions are met. After Closing, many Mortgages keep an escrow account that collects monthly Property Tax and insurance premiums alongside the loan payment, then disburses them when due. Lenders typically require escrow accounts when LTV exceeds 80%.

plain: The federal tax on assets transferred at death — Real Estate held in the estate is included at fair-market value, with a high lifetime exemption sheltering most estates.
snappy: Federal tax on assets transferred at death, including Real Estate at fair-market value.
detail: Estate Tax applies to combined gross-estate value above the lifetime exemption ($13.61M per person in 2024, scheduled to drop to ~$7M in 2026 absent legislation). Rate: 18-40% graduated on amounts above the exemption. Marital deduction defers tax on assets transferred to a surviving spouse. Step-up in Basis at death eliminates Capital Gain on appreciated assets. Real Estate planning strategies: family limited partnerships, qualified personal residence trusts (QPRTs), grantor retained annuity trusts (GRATs), valuation discounts on illiquid Real Estate interests. State-level estate taxes apply in Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington, and DC — with much lower exemption thresholds than federal.

plain: A signed Tenant document confirming key Lease terms — Rent paid, no defaults, no special claims against the Landlord — required at building sale or refinance.
snappy: Tenant-signed certificate confirming Lease terms and stopping later claims that contradict it.
detail: Estoppel certificates protect the buyer or new Lender from surprise post-Closing claims by Tenants. The certificate confirms: current Rent, remaining term, options and renewal rights, no Landlord defaults, no offsets, no oral side agreements, no claims for repairs. Once signed, the Tenant is 'estopped' (legally prevented) from making contradictory claims later. Mandatory at sale of investment property — Lenders won't fund without them from major Tenants. Tenants negotiate certain estoppel exclusions (preserve audit rights, environmental claims). Multifamily transactions sometimes use 'tenant questionnaires' instead.

plain: A metric measuring building energy consumption — kBtu per square foot per year — used for benchmarking and Energy Star certification.
snappy: Building energy consumption per square foot per year — used for benchmarking.
detail: EUI is the standard energy-benchmarking metric. Calculation: total annual energy use ÷ rentable square footage, expressed in kBtu/SF/year. Standard EUI: 80-100 for typical Office, 200-300 for high-energy uses (Data Center, Cold Storage), 50-80 for efficient Office, 20-30 for Passive House Multifamily. Energy Star score: percentile rank based on EUI compared to similar buildings nationally. Reporting: EPA Portfolio Manager benchmarks free for any building owner. Mandatory benchmarking laws: NYC, Boston, Chicago, Philadelphia, Seattle, Washington DC, San Francisco, Atlanta. Carbon-emissions rules (NYC LL97) increasingly drive EUI to centre stage in operations strategy.

plain: The legal process Landlords use to remove a Tenant who has stopped paying rent or breached the Lease.
snappy: Court-ordered removal of a Tenant from a leased property.
detail: Eviction is a court process — Landlords cannot self-help by changing locks, removing belongings, or shutting off utilities. Steps: written notice (3-30 days depending on state and grounds), filing an unlawful-detainer action, court hearing, judgment, and sheriff-enforced removal. Total time runs from 3 weeks (fast states like Texas) to 6+ months (slow states like New York). Tenants can typically cure non-payment evictions by paying owed rent before judgment.

plain: A government order temporarily prohibiting evictions — typically during emergencies — used widely during 2020-2021 COVID pandemic to prevent mass homelessness.
snappy: Government order temporarily prohibiting evictions during emergencies.
detail: Eviction Moratoriums protect Tenants during widespread economic hardship. Federal moratorium: CARES Act (March 2020 — initial 4 months), CDC Eviction Moratorium (September 2020 — August 2021), struck down by Supreme Court August 2021. State moratoriums: California through August 2022, New York through January 2022, Massachusetts through March 2021, multiple others. Landlord impact: extended rent arrears (often without ability to evict), state rental-assistance programs (Emergency Rental Assistance Program, ERAP) compensated some shortfalls. Legacy: ongoing 'just cause eviction' legislation in California, Oregon, and major cities partly reflects moratorium-era political shift.

plain: A Lease provision barring the Landlord from leasing space in the centre to a competing business — protects the Tenant from direct competition next door.
snappy: Lease provision blocking the Landlord from leasing to direct competitors.
detail: Exclusive Use Clauses are the Tenant's defence against in-centre competition. Common in Retail: a grocery store with exclusive against other supermarkets; a dental practice with exclusive against other dentists; a coffee shop with exclusive against competing chains. Landlord scope of restriction depends on Tenant leverage — Anchors get broad exclusives; smaller inline Tenants get narrow ones. Disputes arise: does a CVS prescription counter violate a Walgreen's pharmacy exclusive? Does a Starbucks at an outparcel violate a Dunkin' inline exclusive? Courts interpret narrowly in favour of Landlord flexibility. Modern Retail landlords push for narrower exclusives.

plain: The person named in a will to manage a deceased person's estate — including any Real Estate — through Probate.
snappy: Person named in a will to manage the deceased's estate through Probate.
detail: The Executor (Personal Representative in some states) is responsible for: filing the will with Probate Court, inventorying assets, notifying creditors, paying debts and taxes, managing property during probate, and distributing remaining assets. For Real Estate: maintaining property, paying Property Tax and insurance, sometimes selling property to pay debts or distribute proceeds. Executors carry personal liability for breach of fiduciary duty. Compensation: statutory fees ranging 2-5% of estate.

plain: The Cap Rate assumed at sale at the end of the hold period — drives the projected Sale Price in any underwriting model.
snappy: Cap Rate assumed at projected exit sale, driving the residual value.
detail: Exit cap rate is the most sensitive assumption in any commercial Real Estate underwrite. A 25-basis-point change in Exit Cap moves residual value by 4-5% — enough to flip a deal from win to loss. Conservative underwriting prices Exit Cap above Going-In Cap Rate to reflect normal Cap Rate widening over a typical 5-7 year hold. Aggressive underwriting holds Exit Cap flat or compresses it — a red flag in pro formas. Sensitivity tables in offering memos quantify the range; LPs scrutinise.

plain: A loss in property value caused by factors outside the property — a noisy highway next door, a dying retail strip, a declining neighbourhood — that the owner can't fix.
snappy: Loss in property value from factors outside the property the owner can't change.
detail: External obsolescence is the third leg of Depreciation alongside physical wear and Functional Obsolescence. Examples: a new highway built behind a residential subdivision, an industrial plant moved next door to apartments, a regional employer's relocation gutting demand, neighbourhood decline pushing comparable values down. Always incurable from the property's perspective — the Appraiser deducts it as a value loss in the Cost Approach. The Income Approach and Sales Comparison Approach naturally pick up external obsolescence through depressed rents and falling Comps.

plain: A REIT structure where an outside management company manages operations — earns fees from the REIT — common in mortgage REITs and some non-traded REITs.
snappy: REIT outsourcing operations to a fee-charging external manager.
detail: External Management persists in: mortgage REITs (Apollo, KKR, Annaly externally managed by parent companies), non-traded REITs (often externally managed by Sponsor entities), small specialty REITs. Compensation: management fee (1-1.5% of equity), incentive fee (typically 20% of returns above hurdle). Conflicts: management company shareholders vs REIT shareholders. Activist investor pressure consistently pushes externally-managed REITs toward internalisation. The 2020s era still has 60-80 publicly-traded externally-managed REITs but the model is in long-term decline for transparency and alignment reasons.

plain: The 1968 federal law banning housing discrimination on race, colour, religion, national origin, sex, disability, and family status.
snappy: 1968 federal law banning housing discrimination on protected classes.
detail: The Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination in renting, selling, financing, and advertising housing based on race, colour, religion, national origin, sex, disability, and family status (the seven federal protected classes). Many states and cities add classes — sexual orientation, gender identity, source of income, military status. HUD's Office of Fair Housing investigates complaints. Lenders, Landlords, and real estate Agents face civil and criminal liability for violations.

plain: The largest US government-sponsored buyer of home loans — Lenders sell Mortgages to Fannie Mae and Fannie repackages them for investors.
snappy: Government-sponsored enterprise that buys Conforming Loans from Lenders.
detail: Fannie Mae is a publicly traded but federally chartered company (a government-sponsored enterprise, or GSE) that buys Conforming Loans from Lenders, repackages them into mortgage-backed securities, and sells those to investors. This secondary market provides the liquidity that lets Lenders keep originating new Mortgages. Fannie Mae went into federal conservatorship in 2008 and remains there. Sister entity Freddie Mac plays the same role with slightly different operational rules.

plain: Common shorthand for Floor Area Ratio — the multiplier of Lot size that caps total building floor area under Zoning.
snappy: Standard shorthand for Floor Area Ratio in Zoning analysis.
detail: FAR is the Zoning vocabulary for building density. Pronounced 'far' as one syllable in industry use. Cities publish FAR caps by district — Manhattan downtown FAR can exceed 15; suburban Office parks run 0.3-0.5. Higher-FAR Zoning multiplies Land value because more revenue-generating square footage can fit on the same parcel. See Floor Area Ratio for full mechanics, bonus structures, and how FAR interacts with Setback and height limits.

plain: The most complete form of ownership — you can use the Land, sell it, leave it to heirs, with no time limit.
snappy: Absolute ownership of Real Property with no time limit and full transfer rights.
detail: Fee simple is the default form of US Real Property ownership. The holder can occupy, sell, mortgage, lease, or devise the property without expiration. Restrictions still apply: Zoning, Property Tax, Easements, CC&Rs, and Eminent Domain all bind a fee simple owner. Compare leasehold (a tenant under a Lease has possession but not ownership) and life estate (ownership ends at the holder's death). Almost all single-family homes in the US are sold fee simple.

plain: The movable items inside a building — chairs, desks, beds, appliances, equipment — that aren't part of the Real Property but get included in Sales of Hotels, restaurants, and operating businesses.
snappy: Movable contents of a building — furniture, fixtures, equipment — typically not Real Property.
detail: FF&E sits between Real Property and Personal Property in operating-business Sales. Hotel transactions allocate Purchase Price between FF&E (furniture, beds, soft goods, kitchen equipment, IT gear), Real Property (building, Land), and intangibles (brand, going-concern value). Tax basis allocation matters — FF&E depreciates over 5-7 years (versus 39 years for commercial Real Property), generating front-loaded Depreciation deductions. Hotel and restaurant operators carry FF&E reserves — typically 3-5% of revenue — for periodic replacement of soft goods (every 5-7 years) and hard goods (10-15 years).

plain: The standard REIT operating-metric — net income excluding gains on property sales plus depreciation — used in place of net income for REIT analysis.
snappy: REIT operating-metric net of property-Sale gains, plus depreciation.
detail: Funds From Operations (FFO) is the dominant REIT performance metric. Calculation: Net Income + Depreciation and Amortisation + Losses on Sales − Gains on Sales − Other non-cash items. Why: standard net income understates REIT performance because real estate Depreciation is non-cash and properties don't actually deteriorate in market value. FFO per share is the standard REIT valuation multiple (P/FFO replaces P/E). Nareit defines FFO precisely to enable comparison across REITs. Reported quarterly alongside GAAP earnings. AFFO (Adjusted Funds From Operations) further adjusts for recurring capital expenditures.

plain: The federal agency inside HUD that insures FHA Loans, letting buyers get a Mortgage with only 3.5% down.
snappy: Federal agency inside HUD insuring low-Down-Payment FHA Loans.
detail: The FHA insures Mortgages made to low-Down-Payment borrowers, letting them buy with as little as 3.5% down (or 10% down with Credit Score 500-579). The insurance — funded by borrower-paid MIP — covers Lender losses on Default, which is why Lenders accept lower Credit Scores and Down Payments on an FHA Loan than on a Conventional Loan. Part of HUD; distinct from FHFA (which oversees Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac).

plain: An FHA-insured Mortgage that combines a home purchase or Refinance with funds for renovation — lets buyers acquire and Rehab properties needing work.
snappy: FHA-insured combined purchase-and-Rehab Mortgage for properties needing work.
detail: FHA 203k loans bridge a major gap in residential financing. Two flavours: Standard 203k (renovations over $35,000, requires HUD-approved consultant) and Limited 203k (under $35,000, simpler). Eligible work: structural repairs, modernisation, energy improvements, accessibility upgrades, additions. Excluded: luxury items. Maximum LTV up to 96.5% of as-completed value. Major use case: buyer wants distressed property, needs financing to Rehab without separate construction loan.

plain: A Mortgage insured by the Federal Housing Administration — easier to qualify for and lower Down Payment than conventional.
snappy: FHA-insured Mortgage with 3.5% Down Payment minimum.
detail: FHA Loans require 3.5% Down Payment with a Credit Score of 580+, or 10% down with scores 500-579. Borrowers pay both an upfront mortgage insurance premium (1.75% of loan amount) and an ongoing monthly premium for the life of the loan if Down Payment is under 10%. Loan limits track FHFA Conforming Loan limits but adjusted by county. FHA Loans are Assumable, which became newly valuable after the 2022 rate spike.

plain: An FHA Refinance option that lets existing FHA borrowers Refinance into a lower rate with minimal Underwriting — no Appraisal, no new Credit Score check.
snappy: FHA Refinance option with no Appraisal, no Credit check, no Income verification.
detail: FHA Streamline Refinance is the federal equivalent of VA's IRRRL. Eligibility: existing FHA Loan, current on payments, 6+ months of payments made, Refinance produces 'net tangible benefit' (typically 0.5%+ rate reduction). No Appraisal required. No new Credit Score pull. No employment verification. Process completes in 2-4 weeks. Cost: Closing Costs plus the FHA's 1.75% upfront MIP. Borrower-friendly when rates have dropped significantly.

plain: The federal regulator that oversees Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac — sets the size limits on Conforming Loans.
snappy: Federal regulator of Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Conforming Loan limits.
detail: The FHFA was created in 2008 to oversee the housing GSEs (Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac) plus the Federal Home Loan Banks. It sets the annual Conforming Loan limits, supervises the GSEs' Underwriting standards, and acts as their conservator since the 2008 financial crisis. Publishes the closely-watched FHFA House Price Index quarterly, a key benchmark for residential price trends.

plain: The most widely used Credit Score in US lending — a number from 300 to 850 that summarises a borrower's credit history.
snappy: Industry-standard Credit Score model used by most US mortgage lenders.
detail: FICO scores aggregate five factors: payment history (35%), amounts owed (30%), length of credit history (15%), new credit (10%), credit mix (10%). Mortgage underwriting typically pulls FICO from all three bureaus and uses the middle score for the highest-scoring borrower on the application. Conventional Loans usually need 620+; FHA Loans accept 580+ with 3.5% Down Payment, or 500+ with 10%; VA Loans have no statutory minimum but lender overlays often require 620. Higher scores unlock lower rates and lower PMI premiums.

plain: The construction milestone when all work — including punch-list items — is fully complete and accepted by the owner.
snappy: Construction milestone: all work including punch-list complete and accepted.
detail: Final Completion follows Substantial Completion by weeks to months as the GC works through the punch list. Final Completion triggers: release of the GC's holdback (typically 5-10% of contract value), final payment, end of the GC's lien-filing rights. The owner's architect or owner's representative inspects and certifies Final Completion. Disputes at Final Completion can drag for months — the GC presses for release of holdback while the owner challenges punch-list quality. Lien Waivers from the GC and Subcontractors at Final Completion close the contractor's claims-window on the project.

plain: A loan term requiring the borrower to maintain specific financial metrics — DSCR, LTV, Debt Yield, occupancy — with Defaults triggered by breach.
snappy: Loan term requiring borrower to maintain specific financial metrics throughout the loan.
detail: Financial Covenants give Commercial Lenders early warning and intervention rights as a borrower's financial position deteriorates. Common covenants: minimum DSCR, maximum LTV, minimum Debt Yield, minimum occupancy, minimum net worth (for guarantor), liquidity reserves. Breach triggers: cash management (cash sweep), springing recourse, cure rights, or formal Default. Negative covenants restrict borrower actions: additional debt without Lender consent, transfers without consent, distributions during periods of financial stress, change in management or ownership. Maintenance covenants test continuously; incurrence covenants test only at specific events. Financial covenants are heavily negotiated in middle-market and large CRE loans.

full: Foreign Investment in Real Property Tax Act
plain: The federal law requiring foreign Real Estate sellers to have 15% of Sale Price withheld at Closing — collected toward potential US federal Capital Gain tax.
snappy: Federal law requiring 15% withholding from foreign Real Estate sellers at Closing.
detail: FIRPTA (1980) treats Real Property gains by foreign persons as US-sourced income. The buyer or Closing Agent withholds 15% of Sale Price and remits to the IRS within 20 days. Reduced or zero withholding available with IRS Form 8288-B (withholding certificate) where the actual tax liability would be lower. Foreign sellers can recover overpayment through later US tax return. Affects: foreign nationals selling US property, foreign corporations, foreign-controlled US entities. FIRPTA reduces foreign investor appetite for direct US Real Estate ownership; many use US-corporation blockers to manage.

plain: A buyer purchasing their primary residence for the first time — distinct from repeat buyers — eligible for specific government programs and tax benefits.
snappy: Buyer purchasing first primary residence — eligible for specific programs.
detail: First-Time Homebuyer status unlocks special programs: FHA 3.5% Down Payment Loans (anyone qualifies, but FTHB are typical), state housing-finance-agency Down Payment Assistance, USDA Section 502 Direct Loans, retirement-account withdrawal penalties waived for first-home purchase under $10K, Mortgage Credit Certificate programs. Definition: someone who hasn't owned a primary residence in the prior three years. FTHB share of US Sales: ~30-32% in 2024, down from historical 40% — Affordability constraints and competition from Cash Buyers squeeze the segment. Various First-Time Homebuyer tax-credit proposals consistently fail at federal level.

plain: A Mortgage whose interest rate stays the same for the entire loan term — payment never changes.
snappy: Mortgage with a constant interest rate over the full term.
detail: The 30-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage is the dominant US Mortgage product, available because Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac buy them and bear the prepayment risk. Other terms are 10, 15, 20, and 25 years. The borrower's monthly Principal and Interest payment never changes — only the Property Tax and insurance held in Escrow and insurance adjust. Contrast with an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage, which is cheaper upfront but variable.

plain: An item once Personal Property that's been so attached to a building it now counts as part of the Real Property.
snappy: Personal Property that's been affixed to Real Property and now travels with it.
detail: A ceiling fan was personal property in the box at the hardware store. Once wired into the joists, courts treat it as a fixture — it stays with the house when sold. Common disputes: chandeliers, built-in bookshelves, mounted televisions, washer/dryer hookups. Three-part test: method of attachment, adaptation to the property, intent at the time of installation. Purchase contracts list specific items to exclude (often the kitchen refrigerator) or include to avoid post-Closing arguments.

plain: A Commercial property combining warehouse-style space with office and showroom areas — flexible build-out for small businesses needing both.
snappy: Hybrid warehouse/office property serving small businesses needing flexible space.
detail: Flex Industrial fills the gap between pure warehouse and pure office. Typical flex bays run 2,000-10,000 SF, with 15-22 foot clear heights, drive-in doors or single dock door, and a 20-40% office build-out at the front. Tenants: small distributors, light manufacturers, contractors, biotech and R&D firms in single-floor configurations. Flex performs less volatility than either pure office or pure warehouse — diverse Tenant base, modest unit size, smaller absolute Rent exposure. Distinct from bulk warehouse (single-Tenant, 200,000+ SF) and pure office.

plain: Office space leased under flexible short-term terms — Coworking memberships, short-term subleases, on-demand meeting rooms — distinct from traditional 5-10 year Office Leases.
snappy: Office space under flexible short-term terms — Coworking, subleases, on-demand meeting rooms.
detail: Flex Office grew as Office Tenants sought to match space to actual headcount in hybrid-work era. Standard formats: month-to-month memberships, 3-12 month leases through Coworking operators, on-demand meeting rooms (via Convene, LiquidSpace platforms), sublease takeovers with shortened terms. Tenant benefits: avoid long-term commitments, scale up/down with team size. Landlord challenges: lower per-square-foot revenue than traditional Leases, Tenant concentration in operating partners (WeWork, Industrious), credit-quality concerns. Post-2020 hybrid-work trends accelerated Flex Office adoption; major Office investors now budget Flex Office in pro formas.

plain: A Rate Lock feature letting the borrower capture a lower rate if market rates drop before Closing — usually for a fee or higher upfront pricing.
snappy: Rate Lock feature letting the borrower capture lower rates if market drops before Closing.
detail: Float-down options are the Rate Lock equivalent of buying optionality. Mechanics: borrower locks at, say, 7.0% for 60 days with a float-down option. If market rates drop to 6.5% before Closing, the borrower can exercise the float-down and close at 6.5% (often with a small re-lock fee). If rates rise, the original lock holds. Cost: 12.5-25 basis points priced into the lock, or a flat $300-$500 fee. Useful in falling-rate or volatile environments; useless when rates are rising. Float-downs are more common in retail-channel Mortgages than wholesale.

plain: Insurance covering damage from flooding — usually separate from standard Homeowners Insurance, mostly provided by the federal National Flood Insurance Program in high-risk zones.
snappy: Standalone insurance covering flood damage — mostly federal NFIP in FEMA-mapped flood zones.
detail: Homeowners Insurance excludes flood damage. The federal NFIP (1968) provides most US flood insurance, capped at $250K residential dwelling / $100K contents. Premiums historically set well below true risk — politically subsidised — but FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0 (2021) reset premiums toward actuarial pricing, sharply raising rates for older coastal properties. Private flood policies exist for higher coverage limits and luxury homes outside NFIP caps. Required by Lenders for Mortgages on properties in FEMA-designated Special Flood Hazard Areas. The 2017-2024 hurricane and inland-flood cycle accelerated NFIP losses and reform pressure.

plain: How much total building floor area can fit on a Lot, expressed as a multiplier of Lot size — FAR 2.0 means 200% of the Lot area can be built as floor space across all stories.
snappy: Ratio of buildable floor area to Lot size, set by Zoning.
detail: FAR is the headline density control in urban Zoning. A 10,000 sq ft Lot with FAR 2.0 permits 20,000 sq ft of total floor area — could be 2 stories full-coverage, 4 stories at half-coverage, or some mix. Higher FAR means taller, denser buildings. Manhattan downtown FAR can exceed 15; suburban office parks run 0.3-0.5. Bonuses can lift base FAR (affordable-housing inclusion, public-space contribution, transit proximity). Developers maximise FAR to maximise per-Lot value — the metric drives Land prices in dense markets.

plain: The total floor area on one Office floor — drives Tenant fit, efficiency, and the leasing strategy.
snappy: Total floor area on one Office floor — drives Tenant fit and leasing strategy.
detail: Floor Plates shape Office building strategy. Trophy CBD towers: 20,000-40,000 SF Floor Plates supporting large Tenants. Mid-rise suburban Office: 12,000-25,000 SF supporting multiple Tenants per floor. Smaller boutique buildings: 5,000-10,000 SF, single-Tenant floor configurations possible. Single-Tenant floor occupancy maximises Tenant brand expression; Multi-Tenant floors increase R/U Factor through shared elevator lobby and corridors. Large-Floor-Plate Tenant demand drove the post-2020 surge in dense urban-core leasing while small-Floor-Plate suburban Office struggled.

plain: A temporary pause or reduction in Mortgage payments granted by the Lender during a borrower hardship — repayment is deferred but still owed.
snappy: Temporary lender-approved pause or reduction in Mortgage payments during borrower hardship.
detail: Forbearance differs from Loan Modification — it's temporary, not permanent. Common in three scenarios: natural disaster (federal disaster declarations trigger automatic forbearance offers from federally backed Loans), economic shock (the 2020 CARES Act allowed up to 18 months of forbearance on federally backed Mortgages), individual hardship (job loss, medical). Repayment options at the end: lump sum (rarely used), repayment plan (catch-up over months), Loan Modification rolling missed payments into Principal, partial claim (FHA buys back missed payments). Credit reporting is paused or suppressed during the forbearance.

plain: A Lease provision excusing Landlord or Tenant from performance during specific extraordinary events — hurricanes, wars, government orders — without breach.
snappy: Lease provision excusing performance during extraordinary events without breach.
detail: Force Majeure clauses allocate risk for events beyond either party's control. Standard scope: natural disasters (hurricane, fire, earthquake), wars, terrorism, government orders, strikes. Pre-2020, Force Majeure rarely invoked outside acts of God. The COVID-19 government shutdowns 2020 triggered Force Majeure disputes across Retail and restaurant Leases — courts often interpreted narrowly against Tenants. Post-2020 Lease drafting explicitly addresses pandemic, government shutdown, and supply-chain failure. Tenant burden: prove Force Majeure prevented specific lease obligations. Force Majeure typically doesn't excuse Rent payment unless explicitly stated.

plain: The legal process by which a Lender takes back a property after the borrower stops paying the Mortgage.
snappy: Legal process Lenders use to repossess and sell property after Default.
detail: Foreclosure is triggered by the Acceleration Clause after sustained Default. In Mortgage states, foreclosure is judicial — Lenders sue in court and the process takes 12-24 months on average. In Deed of Trust states the process is non-judicial — the trustee can sell at auction in 3-6 months. After auction, unsold properties become REO on the Lender's books. Foreclosure devastates Credit Scores and bars new federally backed Mortgages for 3-7 years.

plain: The public auction at the end of a Foreclosure proceeding — Real Estate sold to the highest bidder, with proceeds going first to the foreclosing Lender.
snappy: Public auction at the end of Foreclosure — proceeds go first to the Lender.
detail: Foreclosure Sale is the umbrella term for the auction concluding any Foreclosure — Judicial Foreclosure (Sheriff's Sale conducted by the county sheriff after court judgment) or Non-Judicial Foreclosure (Trustee's Sale conducted by the Trustee under power-of-sale clause). The Lender almost always credit-bids up to the loan balance — taking the property at a paper price equal to debt rather than paying cash. Excess proceeds above the loan amount go to junior Lien holders then to the borrower. Most properties revert to the Lender as REO when no third-party bidder exceeds the credit bid.

plain: A non-US-resident individual or entity purchasing US Real Estate — subject to FIRPTA on Sale, restrictions in some states, and specific Title and tax compliance requirements.
snappy: Non-US-resident individual or entity purchasing US Real Estate.
detail: Foreign Buyer activity in US Real Estate concentrates in: gateway cities (NYC, Miami, San Francisco, Los Angeles), luxury condos (Manhattan, Florida coast), commercial trophy assets, distressed-debt opportunities. Major buyer countries: Canada (largest residential buyer source), China, Mexico, India, Brazil. Restrictions: Florida 2023 SB 264 banned certain Chinese buyers from buying near military bases; similar laws spread through state legislatures. Tax: ITIN required for sellers, FIRPTA withholding at Sale (15% of Sale Price typically), special partnership-level withholding on K-1 income. Title companies require additional documentation (passport, foreign tax ID) for foreign buyers.

plain: Fannie Mae's sister GSE — buys Conforming Loans from Lenders and resells them to investors, keeping the Mortgage market liquid.
snappy: Government-sponsored enterprise that buys Conforming Loans, alongside Fannie Mae.
detail: Freddie Mac is the second of the two big housing GSEs alongside Fannie Mae. Created in 1970 to compete with Fannie Mae and add liquidity to the Mortgage market. Buys Conforming Loans from Lenders, securitises them, and publishes the Primary Mortgage Market Survey — the weekly 30-year average rate widely cited in the press. Like Fannie Mae, has been in FHFA conservatorship since 2008.

plain: A loss in property value caused by outdated design, layout, or features — galleys kitchens, low ceilings, no garage, single bathrooms — that buyers no longer want.
snappy: Loss in property value from outdated design, layout, or features inside the building.
detail: Functional obsolescence is the design-side cousin of physical Depreciation. Examples: 8-foot ceilings when the market expects 9-foot, single bathrooms in 4-bedroom homes, drive-through tellers in renovated banks turned offices, narrow Office floor plates that don't suit open-plan layouts, awkward elevator location. Curable functional obsolescence (the cost to fix is less than the value gained) gets accounted for as a renovation budget. Incurable functional obsolescence (cost exceeds gain) gets deducted as a value loss. Distinct from External Obsolescence (which comes from outside the property).

plain: Low-rise Multifamily — typically 2-3 stories — built around green space with surface parking and walking paths — the suburban Multifamily format dominant in the South and West.
snappy: Low-rise 2-3 story Multifamily around green space with surface parking.
detail: Garden Apartment is the suburban Multifamily format. Configuration: 2-3 story walk-up buildings, no elevators, surface parking, central landscaped courtyards, often with on-site amenities (pool, fitness, leasing office). Density: 18-30 units per acre. Construction: Stick-Built Type V wood frame keeps cost low. Common in Sun Belt growth markets (Texas, Florida, Arizona, Atlanta, Charlotte). Investment performance: stable Multifamily fundamentals, modest Cap Rates 4.5-6.5% in major markets.

plain: Common shorthand for a General Contractor — the firm managing all construction work on a project.
snappy: Standard shorthand for General Contractor in construction.
detail: GC is the universal industry shorthand for General Contractor. Owners, architects, Lenders, and Subcontractors all refer to the GC in daily conversation and contract language. See General Contractor for the substantive role, contract structures (stipulated sum, cost-plus, GMP), and how the GC coordinates Subcontractors and certifies progress payments.

plain: The firm hired by the property owner or developer to manage all construction work — coordinates subcontractors, handles permits, delivers the completed building.
snappy: Firm managing all construction work — coordinates Subcontractors and delivers the building.
detail: GCs structure construction projects in one of three ways. Stipulated sum: fixed contract price (low risk to owner, GC absorbs cost overruns). Cost-plus: actual costs reimbursed plus a fee (more transparent, owner bears overrun risk). Guaranteed Maximum Price (GMP): cost-plus with a cap (hybrid). The GC schedules trades (framing, plumbing, electrical, HVAC, finishes), pulls permits, manages inspections, certifies progress payments, manages punch lists. Bonded GCs carry payment and performance bonds protecting the owner if work isn't completed. Pre-construction services are often a separate engagement before the build contract.

plain: The federal tax on lifetime transfers of property — including Real Estate gifted to family or others — with annual exclusions plus the lifetime estate-tax exemption.
snappy: Federal tax on lifetime property transfers, with annual exclusion and lifetime exemption.
detail: Annual Gift Tax exclusion: $18,000 per recipient (2024) — unlimited recipients, doubled for married couples ($36,000 per recipient). Gifts above the annual exclusion erode the unified lifetime exemption ($13.61M in 2024). No tax due until lifetime exemption is fully consumed; then gift-tax rates of 18-40% kick in. Common Real Estate gift strategies: gradual transfer of fractional interests in property to children, qualified personal residence trusts, family limited partnerships with discount-eligible interests. Gift Tax recipients take the donor's Cost Basis — distinct from inheritance (Step-up in Basis at death) — making gifts of highly appreciated Real Estate tax-inefficient compared to estate transfer.

plain: A federal agency that guarantees mortgage-backed securities made of FHA, VA, and USDA loans — full faith and credit of the US government.
snappy: Federal guarantor of MBS made from FHA, VA, USDA loan pools.
detail: Unlike Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac (privately owned GSEs), Ginnie Mae is a wholly federal agency inside HUD. It does not buy loans — instead it guarantees the timely payment of mortgage-backed securities made of government-insured loans (FHA Loan, VA Loan, USDA Loan). The full-faith-and-credit guarantee gives Ginnie MBS the lowest credit risk in the agency MBS space, just above US Treasuries.

plain: A construction contract structure where the GC commits to a maximum price — overruns above that cap fall on the contractor, savings below it usually share with the owner.
snappy: Construction contract with GC-committed price cap and shared-savings split.
detail: GMP contracts (Guaranteed Maximum Price) bridge stipulated-sum and cost-plus. The GC opens its books to the owner (transparent cost reporting) but commits to a maximum price ceiling. Cost overruns above the GMP eat into the GC's fee or come out of contractor pocket. Cost savings below the GMP are shared, typically 50/50 or 75/25 owner-favoured. Used in complex commercial projects where neither stipulated sum (too risky for GC given pricing uncertainty) nor cost-plus (too risky for owner) fits. Pre-construction services and trade buyout transparency are essential to GMP success.

plain: A Retail Lease provision requiring the Tenant to actually operate the store — not just pay Rent — protecting Co-Tenants from a Tenant who pays but doesn't draw traffic.
snappy: Lease provision requiring the Tenant to actually operate, not just pay Rent.
detail: Go-Dark Clauses tackle the 'pay-and-go-dark' problem: a struggling chain might continue Rent but close the store to save operating costs, gutting Co-Tenant traffic. Landlord remedies: recapture rights (terminate the Lease and re-lease), Rent acceleration penalties, exclusive-clause cancellation. Tenant pushback: temporary closures should be permitted (renovation, force majeure, transitions). Standard formulations require continuous operation 'in accordance with usual business practices' or 'as a first-class Retail establishment'. Courts read remedy clauses strictly — Landlords with sloppy drafting lose enforceability.

plain: The Cap Rate at the moment of acquisition — calculated from the in-place NOI divided by the purchase price.
snappy: Cap Rate at purchase: current NOI divided by Sale Price.
detail: Going-in cap rate is the snapshot of yield at acquisition. A 5.5% going-in cap on a Multifamily deal means $5.50 of NOI per $100 of purchase price. Value-add Sponsors target a going-in cap below the Exit Cap Rate — they accept lower yield at purchase, expect to lift NOI through Rehab and re-tenanting, and exit at a higher NOI even at a higher Exit Cap. Going-in cap rates compress when investor capital floods in (2020-2021); they widen when rates rise (2022 onward).

plain: The pre-TRID disclosure form giving borrowers an early estimate of Closing Costs — now replaced by the Loan Estimate for residential loans.
snappy: Pre-2015 mortgage cost disclosure, replaced by the Loan Estimate under TRID.
detail: From 1974 (RESPA) until October 2015, lenders had to give a Good Faith Estimate within three business days of application — itemising every Closing Cost. The TRID rule consolidated GFE and the early TILA disclosure into the Loan Estimate. Commercial Real Estate loans, reverse mortgages, and certain home-equity loans still use GFE-style disclosures. The term remains common shorthand in industry conversation even though the form itself is retired for most residential business.

plain: A Hotel's revenue minus departmental and undistributed operating expenses — sits before fixed charges (Property Tax, insurance) and management fees.
snappy: Hotel revenue net of departmental and undistributed operating expenses, before fixed charges.
