The study inventories building components (Roof, façade, paving, HVAC, elevators, pool, mechanical), estimates remaining useful life and replacement cost for each, then computes annual reserve contributions needed to fund replacements without Special Assessments. Required by statute in California, Florida, Nevada, and a growing list of states. The 2021 Surfside condo collapse intensified reserve-study scrutiny — Florida 2022 reforms mandate reserve funding for structural integrity items, no waiver permitted. Lender Underwriting increasingly looks for current reserve studies as part of HOA review.

plain: The percentage of Multifamily Tenants renewing rather than moving out — drives turnover costs, vacancy, and Lease-up demand.
snappy: Percentage of Multifamily Tenants renewing rather than moving out.
detail: Resident Retention is the operating metric Sponsors push hardest in soft markets. Typical Multifamily turnover: 40-55% per year, retention 45-60%. Pricing Rent at renewal is the central tactical lever: aggressive Rent push lifts in-place Rent but raises turnover; modest Rent restraint preserves retention. Turnover costs: Rent loss during vacancy (1-2 weeks), turnover costs (paint, carpet, cleaning — $1,000-$3,000), broker or marketing costs ($500-$2,000). Each unit turnover costs $3,000-$10,000+ in total. Sponsors who retain 70%+ outperform on NOI growth; those running below 40% see operating headwind even with strong Rent growth.

plain: Real Estate intended primarily as a place for people to live — single-family homes, Condos, townhomes, and small Multifamily.
snappy: Real Estate held primarily for residential occupancy by owners or renters.
detail: Residential Real Estate covers properties intended as primary or secondary residences — Single-Family detached homes, Condos, townhomes, Co-ops, ADUs, and small Multifamily (1-4 units, which still qualify for residential Mortgage products like FHA Loans and VA Loans). 5+ unit Multifamily crosses into Commercial Real Estate for financing and Underwriting purposes. Residential transactions are far higher volume but lower individual size than commercial deals.

plain: A federal law regulating how settlement charges are disclosed and banning kickbacks between Lenders, title companies, and Agents.
snappy: Federal law governing settlement disclosures and prohibiting referral kickbacks.
detail: Enacted 1974. RESPA forces standardised settlement-cost disclosure (now folded into the TRID Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure since 2015), regulates Escrow accounts, and bans Section 8 kickbacks for referrals of settlement services. The line between marketing arrangements and illegal kickbacks remains the most litigated area — the CFPB has fined title companies, Lenders, and Agents tens of millions for violations. Borrowers also get a right to switch settlement providers and limits on Escrow over-collection.

plain: The simplest of USPAP Appraisal report formats — minimal narrative, intended for the client only, not for third-party use.
snappy: USPAP's simplest Appraisal report — minimal narrative, client-only use.
detail: USPAP defines three appraisal report types. Restricted Appraisal Report: minimal narrative, intended only for the named client, no third-party reliance. The Appraiser still develops a full opinion of value internally but reports it in compact form. Lower fee than Summary or Self-Contained reports. Used for: internal portfolio decisions, mortgage qualification screening, property tax appeal support. Not acceptable for most Lender requirements (need Summary or fuller).

plain: A commercial building leased to stores, restaurants, and services — strip centres, big boxes, malls, urban street retail.
snappy: Commercial property leased to consumer-facing stores, restaurants, and services.
detail: Retail subtypes: neighbourhood centre (grocery-anchored), community centre (junior anchor + smaller tenants), power centre (big-box tenants), regional and super-regional mall, lifestyle centre, outlet centre, urban street retail. E-commerce pressure has hit mall and Class B retail hardest; grocery-anchored neighbourhood centres have proven resilient. NNN Leases dominate single-tenant retail. Co-tenancy clauses (a tenant's right to break Lease if an anchor leaves) shape multi-tenant centre risk. Mixed-Use redevelopment of dead malls is a growing 2020s theme.

plain: A 1031 Exchange where the investor buys the replacement property BEFORE selling the relinquished one — solves timing problems but adds complexity and cost.
snappy: 1031 Exchange acquiring replacement property before selling the relinquished — solves timing but is complex.
detail: Reverse 1031 lets an investor lock in a replacement property without losing it to another buyer while waiting to sell the relinquished. Mechanics: a Qualified Intermediary parks (holds title to) either the replacement or relinquished property in an Exchange Accommodation Titleholder (EAT) for up to 180 days while the other side of the trade completes. Cost: $5,000-$15,000 in EAT fees and structuring beyond standard 1031 cost. Strict IRS safe-harbour rules (Rev. Proc. 2000-37) must be followed. Used most often in commercial deals where unique replacement properties demand immediate action and Sales timelines are uncertain.

plain: A Mortgage for homeowners 62 and older that pays them cash from their home Equity — repayment is deferred until the borrower sells, moves out, or dies.
snappy: Senior-only Mortgage paying out home Equity in monthly draws or lump sums; deferred repayment.
detail: Reverse Mortgages let seniors tap home Equity without monthly payments. The HECM (FHA-insured) variant dominates — about 95% of US reverse mortgages. The borrower keeps Title, must occupy as primary residence, and pay Property Tax + Homeowners Insurance. Loan balance grows as Interest accrues and payments are advanced. Repayment is triggered by: sale, owner moving out for 12+ months, owner death. If proceeds exceed the loan, the heirs get the excess; if not, the FHA insurance covers the gap. Origination costs are high (3-5% of loan); rates higher than forward Mortgages.

plain: The headline Hotel performance metric — combines Occupancy Rate and ADR — measuring revenue per available room whether occupied or not.
snappy: Hotel performance metric combining Occupancy Rate and ADR — revenue per available room.
detail: RevPAR is the dominant Hotel metric in trade journalism and investor reporting. Calculation: ADR × Occupancy Rate, OR equivalently, total room revenue ÷ available room-nights. RevPAR captures the full demand picture — a Hotel running 80% Occupancy at $150 ADR (RevPAR $120) outperforms one at 70% Occupancy at $160 ADR (RevPAR $112). RevPAR growth year-over-year is the headline operating story for Hotel REITs. RevPAR excludes ancillary revenue (food, beverage, parking, banquets) — TRevPAR (Total RevPAR) is the broader metric some operators report.

plain: A Tenant's contractual right to match any third-party offer the Landlord receives on the property — the Tenant gets first crack at buying before the Landlord can sell to an outsider.
snappy: Tenant right to match any third-party offer to buy the property — first chance at acquisition.
detail: ROFR gives long-term Tenants protection against unwanted property sale to a competitor or hostile owner. Mechanics: Landlord receives a bona-fide offer from a third party; sends the terms to the Tenant; Tenant has a window (typically 30-60 days) to accept identical terms; if Tenant declines, Landlord can sell to the third party (but not at different terms without restarting the process). Common in: Hotel ground Leases, long-term Single-Tenant Net Lease Property, ground Leases. Distinct from Right of First Offer (Tenant gets first chance to buy at the Landlord's set price, not first chance to match a third party).

plain: A defaulted borrower's statutory right to recover the property after Foreclosure Sale by paying the outstanding debt plus costs — varies sharply by state, often months or years long.
snappy: Defaulted borrower's right to recover the property after Foreclosure by paying off the debt.
detail: Right of Redemption comes in two flavours. Equitable Redemption: pre-Sale, the borrower can stop Foreclosure at any time before the auction by paying off the full loan plus arrears and costs. Universally available; the heart of the Foreclosure cure process. Statutory Redemption: post-Sale, in some states the borrower (or junior Lien holders) can repurchase the property within a statutory period (3-12 months typical) by paying the auction price plus statutory Interest and fees. Statutory redemption is available in most Judicial Foreclosure states; absent in most Non-Judicial Foreclosure states. Redemption rights make post-Sale ownership uncertain for periods.

plain: A Multifamily operations practice that bills Tenants for utilities based on a formula (unit size, occupants, square footage) rather than individual sub-metering — captures revenue from utilities without unit-level meters.
snappy: Multifamily billing system charging Tenants for utilities by formula, not individual meters.
detail: RUBS lets Multifamily owners recover utility costs without installing unit-level meters. The formula allocates water, sewer, trash, sometimes gas across units based on bedroom count, square footage, or occupants. Pros: $20-$60/unit/month recovery without capex. Cons: Tenants resist (no incentive to conserve), state regulations limit RUBS in some jurisdictions (California, New York, Florida have restrictions), legal challenges over fairness. Submetering (actual per-unit meters) is the cleaner solution but requires significant Cap-Ex. RUBS revenue lifts NOI by 1-3% in stabilised Multifamily — value-add Sponsors often install RUBS as a quick NOI gain.

plain: What the property actually sold for — the number on the recorded Deed, not the original asking price.
snappy: Final agreed price at which a property changed hands.
detail: Sale Price is the dollar amount in the executed purchase contract, paid by the Buyer and received by the Seller (net of any concessions or credits). The Sale Price appears on the recorded Deed in most jurisdictions and is used to compute Property Tax transfer fees. List-to-Sale ratio compares Sale Price to the seller's original asking price — a market-temperature indicator (>100% = bidding war; <95% = soft market).

plain: A transaction where the property owner sells the building and simultaneously signs a long-term Lease to stay as a Tenant — freeing capital while keeping operational use.
snappy: Owner-occupier sells the property and simultaneously becomes long-term Tenant under a Lease.
detail: Sale-leasebacks are a Commercial Real Estate financing tool. The owner (often a corporate operating business) frees up trapped capital by selling Real Estate to an investor (often a Triple Net Lease REIT) and signs a 10-25 year NNN Lease back at market or above-market Rent. Common in: retail chains, industrial manufacturing, healthcare, hotel operators. Tax considerations are complex — TCJA limits on rent deductibility for sale-leasebacks with above-market Rent. Lease-versus-buy analysis weighs the cost of capital trade-off. STORE Capital, Spirit Realty Capital, and Realty Income built large portfolios around sale-leaseback origination.

plain: An Appraisal method that values a property by what similar properties have recently sold for — the everyday approach for residential homes.
snappy: Appraisal method valuing a property against recent sales of comparable properties.
detail: The sales comparison approach is the dominant residential Appraisal method. The Appraiser identifies three to six recent comparable sales (Comps), adjusts each upward or downward for differences in size, condition, location, age, and features, and reconciles the adjusted prices to estimate the subject's value. USPAP requires the Appraiser to bracket — using Comps that are both above and below the subject in each attribute. Strongest where there is a robust market of similar properties; weakest for unique properties or thin markets.

plain: The entry-level Real Estate licence — required in every US state — letting the holder represent buyers and sellers under supervision of a licensed Broker.
snappy: Entry-level Real Estate licence allowing representation under Broker supervision.
detail: Salesperson Licence requirements vary by state. Typical: 60-180 hours of pre-licensing coursework, state-administered exam, background check, sponsoring Broker affiliation. Continuing education: 8-30 hours every 1-2 years. Salespersons cannot operate independently — must work under a sponsoring Broker who carries E&O Insurance and holds escrow funds. Distinct from Broker Licence (which has higher requirements). Commercial Agents typically hold salesperson licences in early career.

plain: The combined state and local taxes a homeowner pays — capped at $10,000 of federal deduction since the 2017 TCJA.
snappy: Combined state and local tax burden — federal deduction capped at $10,000 since TCJA.
detail: Before 2018, homeowners could deduct unlimited Property Tax plus state income tax against federal income. The TCJA capped the SALT deduction at $10,000 — a major hit to high-Property-Tax states (New York, New Jersey, California, Illinois, Massachusetts). High-income owners in those states lost five-to-six-figure deductions. Multiple states designed workaround entity-level pass-through taxes for business income (PTET), but residential homeowners have no equivalent escape. SALT-cap repeal has been a recurring political flashpoint; through 2024 the cap survived intact.

plain: The $10,000 limit on the federal deduction for state and local taxes — including Property Tax — imposed by the 2017 TCJA.
snappy: $10,000 federal deduction cap on state and local taxes including Property Tax.
detail: SALT Cap is the most punishing TCJA provision for high-Property-Tax-state residents. Federal income tax allows itemised deductions for state income tax plus Property Tax, capped at $10,000 combined since 2018. High-cost states (New York, New Jersey, California, Illinois, Massachusetts, Connecticut) face the brunt. Workarounds: pass-through entity tax (PTET, permitted for business income). Repeal attempts consistently fail. Scheduled to sunset 2026 absent congressional action.

plain: A Small Business Administration-backed Mortgage used by owner-occupiers to buy or build commercial property — lower Down Payment and longer term than conventional CRE financing.
snappy: SBA-backed Mortgage for owner-occupiers of commercial property.
detail: SBA 7(a) and 504 Loans dominate small-business CRE financing. 7(a) covers any business purpose including Real Estate up to $5M, with SBA guaranteeing 75-85% of the loan amount. 504 specifically funds Real Estate or equipment with a structure: 50% bank first-lien, 40% SBA second-lien, 10% borrower Down Payment. Terms: 25 years on Real Estate, fixed-rate 504, variable 7(a). Owner-occupancy: 51%+ of square footage must be used by the owner's business. Common Tenants: dentists, restaurants, professional services, light manufacturing. Conventional CRE Mortgages require 25-35% Down Payment versus SBA's 10% — a major affordability gain for small businesses.

plain: A federal tax break letting homeowners exclude up to $250,000 ($500,000 married filing jointly) of Capital Gain from the sale of a primary residence.
snappy: Federal tax break excluding up to $250K/$500K Capital Gain on primary-residence sale.
detail: IRC §121 lets a homeowner exclude $250,000 ($500,000 married filing jointly) of Capital Gain from federal tax on the sale of a primary residence, provided the seller owned and used the home as principal residence for at least 24 months of the 60 months ending on the sale date. The exclusion can be reused every two years. Doesn't apply to investment property — that's where 1031 Exchange comes in. Partial exclusion is available for early sales due to change of employment, health, or unforeseen circumstances. The cap hasn't been adjusted for inflation since 1997 — high-price-market sellers increasingly exceed it.

plain: A 20% federal tax deduction for income earned through pass-through entities like LLCs and partnerships — created by the 2017 TCJA, includes most Real Estate Investment.
snappy: 20% federal deduction for qualified business income from pass-through entities, including most Real Estate.
detail: Section 199A of the Internal Revenue Code, added by TCJA, gives a 20% deduction on Qualified Business Income (QBI) from pass-through entities (sole proprietorships, partnerships, S corps, LLCs). Most Real Estate rental income qualifies under the 199A safe harbour (250+ hours of services per year, separate books and records, plus contemporaneous records). Limits kick in at higher incomes — Specified Service Trades or Businesses (SSTBs) phase out the deduction, but Real Estate generally isn't SSTB. Scheduled to sunset 2026 absent congressional renewal.

plain: The HUD program funding capital and rental subsidy for very-low-income elderly housing — distinct from market-rate Senior Housing.
snappy: HUD program for very-low-income elderly housing — capital plus rental subsidy.
detail: HUD Section 202 funds Affordable Housing specifically for very-low-income seniors aged 62+. Two components: capital advance (zero-interest forgivable loan covering construction/Rehab) plus Project Rental Assistance Contract (PRAC, monthly rental subsidy covering operating costs and Tenant Rent below 30% of income). Sponsor must be a nonprofit. Roughly 400,000 units nationwide. Limited new construction since 2011 — annual appropriations support primarily existing-property Renovation. Section 811 (disabled-housing equivalent) operates similarly.

plain: The federal rent-subsidy program that helps low-income Tenants pay private-market Rent — vouchers cover the gap between income and Rent.
snappy: Federal rent subsidy paid to private Landlords on behalf of low-income Tenants.
detail: Section 8 (formally the Housing Choice Voucher Program, codified in Section 8 of the Housing Act of 1937 as amended) is the largest federal rental-assistance program — roughly 2.3 million households served. Tenants pay 30% of adjusted income; HUD pays the rest, up to a metro-area payment standard. Local public-housing authorities administer. Landlord acceptance is voluntary in most states; a growing list of states and cities bar Section-8 refusal as discrimination. Tenant turnover in Section-8 units is markedly lower than market — a feature that draws some private Landlords in.

plain: The portable rental-assistance voucher held by Section 8 Tenants — letting them rent in the private market at any property where the Landlord accepts the voucher.
snappy: Portable Section 8 voucher letting Tenants rent in the private market.
detail: Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher is the dominant federal rental-assistance program — roughly 2.3M households nationwide. Eligible Tenant pays 30% of adjusted income; HUD pays the rest up to the Fair Market Rent for the area. Tenant chooses the unit; Landlord must consent to accept the voucher (voluntary in most states, increasingly required by anti-discrimination ordinances). Tenant turnover in Section-8 units markedly lower than market — a feature that draws some private Landlords.

plain: Money the Tenant pays upfront, held by the Landlord to cover damage or unpaid Rent at the end of the Lease.
snappy: Upfront deposit held by Landlord to secure Tenant performance under the Lease.
detail: State statutes cap residential security deposits at 1–2 months of Rent and require return (with itemised deductions) within 14–60 days of move-out. Some states require the deposit to sit in an interest-bearing escrow account, with interest paid to the Tenant. Wrongful withholding triggers statutory damages — often 2–3x the deposit plus attorney's fees. Commercial deposits face fewer statutory constraints; landlords often demand letters of credit or guarantees in addition to or instead of cash deposits.

plain: The most comprehensive USPAP Appraisal report format — full narrative, all supporting data and analysis included — used for high-stakes valuations.
snappy: USPAP's most comprehensive Appraisal report — full narrative with supporting data.
detail: Self-Contained reports lay out the full Appraisal analysis: subject description, market area analysis, all three valuation approaches (Sales Comparison, Income, Cost), reconciliation, supporting Comps with adjustments, exhibits. Length: 100-300+ pages. Required for large commercial transactions, Estate Tax valuations on substantial estates, Eminent Domain proceedings, mortgage transactions over $1M-$5M, divorce or litigation. Higher fee ($5,000-$30,000+) than Restricted or Summary.

plain: Any Landlord attempt to evict a Tenant outside the formal Eviction process — Lockouts, utility shutoffs, harassment — virtually always illegal in US residential rentals.
snappy: Illegal Landlord attempt to evict Tenant outside formal Eviction process.
detail: Self-Help Eviction tactics — Lockouts, shutting off utilities, removing Tenant property, harassment, threats — are prohibited in nearly every US state. Allowed Landlord actions in Lease Default: written notice of cure or quit, filing formal Eviction action, obtaining court judgment, lawful execution via sheriff. Self-Help Eviction penalties: punitive damages, Tenant entitlement to remain in property, statutory damages (often 2-3x actual damages plus attorney's fees), criminal charges in some jurisdictions. Commercial Tenants have weaker self-help protections than residential — some states allow narrow commercial Lockouts on Lease Default.

plain: A property with rentable storage units for personal or business goods — small individual units rented month-to-month, low operating costs, recession-resilient.
snappy: Commercial property of rentable storage units, mostly month-to-month — recession-resilient.
detail: Self-storage emerged as an institutional asset class through the 2000s and accelerated post-2010 with REITs like Public Storage, Extra Space, CubeSmart, and Life Storage. Operating Expenses are unusually low (often 25-35% of revenue) — minimal staffing (one office worker, automated gates), no Tenant Improvement, no HVAC in most unit types. Move-out cycles are constant but turnover costs are trivial. Demand is structural — household downsizing, life-event-driven (death, divorce, downsize, dislocation). Performed strongest in the sector through the 2008 recession and the 2020 pandemic.

plain: Real Estate-specific term for an individual Self-Storage building — distinct from Self-Storage (the asset class) — used for transaction descriptions.
snappy: Individual Self-Storage building used for transaction descriptions.
detail: Self-Storage Facility distinguishes the individual property from the Self-Storage asset class. Typical facility: 50,000-150,000 SF rentable, 500-1,500 units, drive-up access at ground level, climate-controlled units inside. Construction: simple metal-and-concrete construction; per-square-foot cost runs $40-$80, low for Real Estate. Operating intensity: minimal — automated gates, one office staffer, contracted maintenance. Cap Rates: 5-6.5% for institutional-quality facilities. Major Self-Storage REITs: Public Storage, Extra Space Storage, CubeSmart, Life Storage. Asset class consistently outperforms broader Real Estate through cycles.

plain: The party transferring ownership of a property — represented in the transaction by a Listing Agent.
snappy: Party transferring property in a real estate transaction.
detail: The Seller is the party transferring the property — an individual, a couple, an estate, an LLC, or a corporation. In most residential transactions the Seller works through a Listing Agent under a Listing Agreement. The Seller signs the Deed, pays the agreed Commission split from sale proceeds, and is bound by required Disclosure laws. Sellers may also offer concessions (credits at Closing) to sweeten an offer.

plain: Residential property purpose-built for older adults — independent living, assisted living, memory care, skilled nursing — a specialty Commercial asset class.
snappy: Specialty Multifamily for older adults across independent, assisted, memory care, and skilled-nursing tiers.
detail: Senior housing spans an acuity spectrum. Independent living (55+ communities, minimal services). Assisted living (meals, light medical, daily activities — most common subtype). Memory care (secured dementia units). Skilled nursing (medical care, Medicare/Medicaid reimbursed). Demand is demographically driven by ageing baby boomers. Operating intensity is high — labour 50-60% of revenue. Healthcare REITs (Welltower, Ventas, HCP) hold the largest institutional portfolios. Sector took a significant 2020-2021 hit from pandemic mortality and operating cost spikes; recovered through 2023.

plain: The contractual right to collect Mortgage payments — a tradable asset valued at a percentage of the loan balance.
snappy: Contractual right to collect Mortgage payments — bought and sold as a tradable financial asset.
detail: MSR is a major asset class for specialty firms. The servicing fee runs roughly 25 basis points of the outstanding Mortgage balance — split between the servicer's costs and profit. The value of an MSR portfolio fluctuates with Interest rates: when rates rise, fewer Mortgages prepay, so MSR portfolios become more valuable; when rates fall, prepay risk spikes and MSRs lose value. Listed MSR holders: Mr. Cooper, PHH Mortgage, Mid-America Mortgage. Bank holding-company MSR portfolios are subject to Basel III capital rules — a constraint pushing more MSR to non-banks since 2014.

plain: The minimum required distance between a building and the property line — front, side, and rear — set by local Zoning.
snappy: Minimum distance between a building and the Lot line, set by Zoning.
detail: Setbacks shape the buildable envelope on every Lot. Single-family zones typically require 20-30 foot front, 5-15 foot side, 20-30 foot rear setbacks. Corner Lots have two front setbacks. Reduced setbacks are common in dense urban zones and for accessory structures. Building inside the setback creates an Encroachment requiring a Variance or removal. Setback violations are caught at Building Permit review or by a current Survey. Special setbacks apply to wetlands, slopes, easements, and historic districts.

plain: The neutral third party — Title Company, attorney, or escrow company — conducting the Closing process, handling funds, recording documents, and ensuring proper transfer.
snappy: Neutral third party conducting Closing — handles funds, records documents, ensures transfer.
detail: Settlement Agents conduct Closings depending on state custom. Title Company states (much of the South and West): Settlement Agent is typically a Title Insurance underwriter or affiliated company. Attorney states (NY, MA, GA, NJ, much of the Northeast): each side has an attorney; both attorneys plus Title Insurance underwriter participate. Escrow company states (California, parts of West): independent escrow companies serve as neutral third parties. Roles: collect funds from buyer and Lender, pay off prior Liens, record Deed and Mortgage, distribute seller proceeds, ensure ALTA Best Practices compliance. Wire Fraud prevention is now a central responsibility.

plain: A line-by-line tally of every dollar at Closing — who pays what to whom — given to both Buyer and Seller.
snappy: Itemised list of all charges and credits at Closing for Buyer and Seller.
detail: Pre-TRID this was the HUD-1 statement, used for both residential and commercial. Since 2015, residential transactions use the Closing Disclosure; the ALTA Settlement Statement remains the standard for commercial deals and many investor purchases. The form shows Sale Price, Lender charges, title fees, recording fees, transfer taxes, Property Tax prorations, HOA prorations, and the final cash to close. Both sides sign at Closing. Discrepancies between Loan Estimate and final settlement statement above certain tolerances trigger TILA rescission rights.

plain: The county-sheriff-conducted auction at the end of a Judicial Foreclosure — Real Estate is sold to the highest bidder, often the Lender by credit bid.
snappy: County-sheriff-conducted auction ending Judicial Foreclosure proceedings.
detail: Sheriff's Sale is the Judicial Foreclosure equivalent of Trustee's Sale. After the court enters judgment, the Sheriff publishes notice (typically newspaper ads for 3-6 weeks), conducts a public auction at the courthouse steps or designated location, and conveys Title via Sheriff's Deed. The Lender almost always credit-bids up to the outstanding loan balance. Bidder protections: as-is condition (no warranties), buyer responsibility for prior Liens, Quiet Title issues common. Sheriff's Sale produces a brief frenzy of investor activity in distressed markets; most properties revert to Lenders as REO when no third-party bidder exceeds the credit bid.

plain: Selling a home for less than what's owed on the Mortgage, with the Lender agreeing to accept the shortfall instead of foreclosing.
snappy: Sale of property for less than the outstanding Mortgage with lender approval.
detail: A short sale is the polite alternative to Foreclosure. The owner negotiates with the Lender to accept a Sale Price below the loan balance and forgive the deficiency. Approval takes weeks to months — the lender wants proof of hardship, valuation evidence, and a buyer at market price. Forgiven debt is typically taxable as income, though the Mortgage Forgiveness Debt Relief Act provided periodic exemptions during the post-2008 crisis. Credit impact is significant but less severe than a completed Foreclosure.

plain: A commercial Lease where the Tenant pays Property Tax in addition to Base Rent — the simplest Net Lease structure.
snappy: Commercial Lease where Tenant pays Property Tax beyond Base Rent.
detail: Single Net Lease (N Lease) is the entry-level Net Lease structure. The Tenant pays Base Rent plus Property Tax — but Landlord retains insurance and Common Area Maintenance obligations. Rare in modern Commercial Real Estate — most deals are Modified Gross Lease (split obligations) or Triple Net Lease (Tenant pays everything). Single Net survives in small-market Office, some Industrial, and Tenant-favorable Lease negotiations where the parties don't push for full triple-net structure. Tenant accepts Property Tax risk (the most predictable Operating Expense category) while preserving Landlord operating burden on insurance and maintenance.

plain: A detached home on its own Lot, designed for one household — the dominant US housing form.
snappy: Detached home on its own Lot, designed for a single household.
detail: Single-Family detached homes dominate the US housing stock, especially in suburbs. Each home sits on its own Lot, with no shared walls. Distinct from townhomes (attached but separately owned), Condos (units inside a larger building), and Multifamily (multiple rental units in one structure). Zoning that allows only single-family use is the most common American residential land-use designation — and the subject of recent reform debates in many cities.

plain: A house rented out as an investment — single-family detached homes that are owner-financed as investment property rather than primary residences.
snappy: Detached house held as rental investment rather than owner-occupied primary residence.
detail: SFR emerged as an institutional asset class after 2008 — Blackstone (Invitation Homes), American Homes 4 Rent, Tricon, Progress Residential bought tens of thousands of foreclosed homes at distressed prices, professionalised management, and built rent-tracking platforms. The asset class differs from Multifamily: higher per-unit operating costs (per-unit infrastructure, geographically scattered), longer Tenant tenure (3-5+ years versus 1-2 in Multifamily), Rent growth tracking Single-Family home prices rather than apartment markets. Build-to-Rent (BTR) communities — purpose-built SFR neighbourhoods — are the 2020s' fastest-growing SFR subsector.

plain: Full spelling of SPE — a legal entity formed exclusively to hold one Real Estate property.
snappy: Full spelling of SPE — entity holding one specific Real Estate property.
detail: Single-Purpose Entity is the formal name for an SPE — universal in Commercial Real Estate finance. See SPE for the substantive structural requirements, the Bankruptcy Remote rationale, and how SPEs interact with parent-company guarantees and recourse obligations.

plain: An architect-drawn map showing how a proposed building sits on its Lot — Setbacks, parking, landscape, drainage, utilities — submitted for municipal approval.
snappy: Map showing how a proposed building sits on its Lot — submitted for approval.
detail: Site plans are the primary document in any Development approval. They show: building footprint and Setbacks, parking layout and counts, vehicular and pedestrian circulation, landscape and tree protection, drainage and stormwater management, utility connections, signage. Municipalities review for code compliance and design-review-board criteria. Major projects undergo 6-18 months of site-plan review; minor amendments take weeks. Variance applications and Conditional Use Permits often accompany site-plan submission when the proposal deviates from Zoning baseline.

plain: The hospitality-data company providing industry-standard ADR, Occupancy Rate, and RevPAR benchmarks — acquired by CoStar Group and now part of CoStar's broader Real Estate data platform.
snappy: Hotel industry-data company providing ADR, Occupancy, RevPAR benchmarks — now part of CoStar.
detail: Smith Travel Research (STR) founded in 1985 became the de facto benchmark for US Hotel performance. The company collected weekly operating data from member Hotels, anonymised it, and produced market and Comp Set reports. CoStar Group acquired STR in 2019 for $450M, folding it into CoStar's broader CRE-data ecosystem alongside Office, Retail, Industrial, and Multifamily data. STR reports drive Hotel investor pro formas, brand-standard reporting, and operating-team incentive structures. The brand 'STR' persists in industry conversation even though the entity is now CoStar Hospitality.

plain: A three-party agreement among Landlord, Tenant, and Lender that subordinates the Lease to the Mortgage while protecting the Tenant from being evicted on Foreclosure.
snappy: Three-party agreement subordinating Lease to Mortgage with Tenant non-eviction protection.
detail: SNDA balances Lender and Tenant interests. Subordination: the Lease ranks below the Mortgage, so the Lender can Foreclose without preserving Tenant rights. Non-disturbance: but on Foreclosure, the Tenant continues to occupy and pay Rent to the new owner (the Lender or buyer) under the original Lease terms. Attornment: the Tenant agrees to recognise the new owner as Landlord. Without an SNDA, a Lender could Foreclose and terminate Leases — Tenants paying above-market Rent would walk, gutting the property's value. Most investment-grade Commercial Tenants require SNDAs as condition of Lease signing.

plain: The replacement benchmark for LIBOR — what most Adjustable-Rate Mortgages now reset to.
snappy: Treasury-repo-based benchmark replacing LIBOR for ARM resets.
detail: SOFR is the Federal Reserve's chosen LIBOR successor — derived from actual overnight Treasury repo transactions rather than the survey-of-bank-quotes process that made LIBOR manipulable. The New York Fed publishes SOFR daily. Mortgages reference 30-day average SOFR (a backwards-looking compounded rate) plus Margin. SOFR is mechanically slightly different from LIBOR — typically lower, less volatile — so legacy LIBOR loans converted via a federally legislated spread adjustment.

plain: Construction project costs that aren't physical building materials or labour — architecture, engineering, permitting, financing fees, insurance, project management, accounting.
snappy: Construction-project costs other than physical materials and labour — architecture, fees, permits.
detail: Soft Costs typically run 15-25% of total project cost for ground-up commercial construction. Categories: architecture and engineering design (6-10%), permitting and impact fees (1-5%), construction loan Interest (3-6%), legal (1-2%), project management (2-4%), insurance (1-2%), accounting and tax (0.5-1%), marketing and leasing commissions (1-3%). Soft Costs capitalise into Cost Basis under §263A for tax purposes. Sponsor pro formas should bracket Soft Cost ranges carefully — overruns here are common but rarely catastrophic. Hard Costs (materials and labour) make up the remaining 75-85% of project cost.

plain: A property right protecting Solar access — preventing neighbours from blocking sunlight to solar panels — increasingly recognised by state law in solar-friendly jurisdictions.
snappy: Property right protecting Solar access from neighbour blocking.
detail: Solar Easements protect solar-energy property investments. Voluntary Solar Easements: negotiated between neighbours, granting one party rights to sunlight across the other's property. Statutory Solar Access laws: California, New Mexico, Massachusetts, Wisconsin, and others restrict HOAs and neighbours from blocking solar installations. Federal: FCC OTARD rules apply to some installation rights. Real-world conflicts: tree growth blocking neighbour solar, new construction shadowing existing solar, HOA rules banning solar panels. Solar Easements can be recorded for permanence; transferable with the property.

plain: On-site electricity generation using photovoltaic panels — typically rooftop or carport installations — reduces utility consumption and increasingly required by state codes.
snappy: On-site electricity generation using photovoltaic panels — rooftop or carport installations.
detail: Solar Panel Systems generate on-site electricity. Common configurations: residential rooftop (5-10 kW typical), commercial flat-roof arrays (50-500 kW), large commercial carports (200-2,000 kW), utility-scale field deployments (10+ MW). Cost: $2.50-$3.50 per installed watt residential, $1.50-$2.50 commercial. Financial structures: cash purchase, Loan, Solar Power Purchase Agreement (PPA — third party owns panels, sells electricity at fixed rate), solar Lease. Net Metering: utility credits excess generation against future consumption. State incentives: California Solar Initiative, NY-Sun, Massachusetts SMART, ITC federal tax credit. New construction mandates: California requires solar on new homes since 2020.

plain: A legal entity — typically an LLC — formed for the single purpose of holding one specific Real Estate property, with restrictions on other activities and debt.
snappy: Legal entity holding one specific Real Estate property with restricted other activities.
detail: SPE structures are mandatory in CMBS Loans and common in institutional Real Estate. Required restrictions: only one property held, no other business activities, separate books and bank accounts, no commingling with affiliates, independent directors with consent rights over bankruptcy filing, restricted debt (only the senior Mortgage and limited specified subordinate debt). The structure achieves Bankruptcy Remote status. Drawbacks: administrative overhead, restrictions on Sponsor cash management, intercreditor complexity if Mezzanine layered on.

plain: A new house a builder constructs before having a buyer — built on the speculation it will sell during or after construction.
snappy: New house built by a developer on speculation, before any buyer is in contract.
detail: Spec homes sit between custom-build (designed for a specific buyer) and tract development (master-planned community of many similar homes). The builder selects floor plan, finishes, and the Lot before any buyer is identified. Risk: carrying costs (land debt, construction debt, Property Tax, insurance) accumulate until sale. Reward: full retail margin captured without buyer customisation discounts. Spec homes proliferate in hot markets and disappear in cold ones. Builders often pre-list during framing to capture early buyers who want to select finishes mid-build at a discount to true custom pricing.

plain: A one-time charge on property owners — by a city or an HOA — for specific improvements like a new sewer line, sidewalk, or roof replacement.
snappy: One-time charge for specific property improvements, levied by HOA or municipality.
detail: Municipal special assessments fund public improvements that benefit a defined district — sidewalks, sewer mains, sometimes lighting. They appear as a separate line on the Property Tax bill or as a private bond payment. HOA and Condo special assessments cover capital projects (roof, elevator, parking lot) that exceed the reserve fund. Buyers should ask for two years of HOA financials and minutes to see pending special assessments — an unfunded $30,000 roof can derail a deal. Disclosure is mandatory in most states.

plain: The CMBS-specific party that takes over a distressed Mortgage from the regular Master Servicer — has discretion to modify, extend, sell, or foreclose on behalf of bondholders.
snappy: CMBS party taking over distressed Mortgages from the Master Servicer — workout authority.
detail: Special Servicers manage CMBS Loans in or near Default. The Master Servicer handles routine collection on performing Loans; once a Loan is 60+ days delinquent or the borrower triggers specific events, control transfers to the Special Servicer. Major Special Servicers: LNR Partners (largest), Rialto Capital, KeyBank, Greystone. The Special Servicer's fiduciary duties run to the CMBS bondholders, not the Lender brand. Borrowers complain Special Servicers move too slowly, charge high fees, and prefer Foreclosure over modification. CMBS regulators and rating agencies monitor Special Servicer performance — failures during 2008-2012 produced major reform of conflict-of-interest rules.

plain: A geographic area where property owners pay extra taxes to fund specific improvements or services — schools, sewers, parks, infrastructure — beyond standard municipal services.
snappy: Geographic area where property owners pay extra taxes for specific improvements or services.
detail: Special Tax Districts (also Special Assessment Districts) are common throughout the US. Categories: school district overlays, water and sewer districts, park districts, lighting districts, transit improvement districts, business improvement districts (BIDs). Funding mechanism: line item on the annual Property Tax bill, separate from standard tax. Common in: new residential subdivisions where developers structure long-term infrastructure payback, downtown business areas where BIDs fund extra services. Property buyers should review all special assessment line items during Due Diligence — they can add $500-$5,000+/year to Property Tax.

plain: A Deed where the seller warrants only the period of their own ownership — not the full Chain of Title — common in commercial transactions and tax sales.
snappy: Deed warranting only against defects arising during seller's ownership, not prior chain.
detail: Special Warranty Deed is the middle ground between Warranty Deed (broad warranties going back forever) and Quitclaim Deed (no warranties at all). The grantor warrants only against defects that arose during their ownership — not defects predating it. Common in: commercial transactions where the seller refuses unlimited indemnification, tax sales (the state never had earlier history to warrant), estate sales by executors. Buyers protect against pre-grantor defects via Title Insurance. Texas, Florida, and some Western states call this 'Special Warranty Deed' as the dominant residential conveyance form, blurring the residential convention elsewhere.

plain: A REIT or operating company distribution of a subsidiary's stock to existing shareholders — separating two businesses without a Sale.
snappy: Distribution of a subsidiary's stock to existing shareholders, separating two businesses.
detail: REIT spin-offs unlock value where management of two businesses creates dis-synergy. Notable examples: Penn National's gaming Real Estate into GLPI (2013), Darden's Olive Garden Real Estate into Four Corners (2015), Marriott's Hotel real estate from operating businesses (multiple), Ryman Hospitality's spin-out from operations. Tax-free under IRC §355 if structured correctly — five-year operating-purpose requirement and other rules. Shareholders end up with stock in both the parent and the spin-off proportional to their parent holdings. The spin-off often outperforms the parent post-separation as separated focus drives execution.

plain: The active manager of a Real Estate syndication — finds the deal, raises equity, oversees operations, and earns a Promote for performance.
snappy: Active partner running a Real Estate syndication — origination, operations, and execution.
detail: The Sponsor is the GP in a typical Real Estate LP structure. Brings the deal, leads due diligence, executes the business plan, manages day-to-day operations, communicates with Limited Partners. Earns three layers of compensation: acquisition fee (1-2% of purchase price), asset-management fee (1-2% of equity per year), and a Promote (share of profits above an IRR hurdle). LPs underwrite the Sponsor track record, alignment of interests, and reporting discipline as carefully as the deal itself. Bad Sponsors lose investor capital regardless of market.

plain: A Commercial Mortgage provision that automatically triggers a Cash Trap when defined conditions occur — DSCR breach, occupancy decline, lease expiration concentration.
snappy: Loan provision auto-triggering Cash Trap when defined conditions occur.
detail: Springing Cash Sweeps automate stress responses in Commercial Mortgages. Typical triggers: DSCR <1.20x for any quarter, occupancy <85%, more than 25% of Rent expiring within 18 months without renewal commitments, Major Tenant Default (specific Tenants identified at Loan origination), failure to fund Reserve Accounts, breach of financial reporting requirements. On Trigger: cash management activates, excess cash flow sweeps to Reserve, borrower distributions cease. Off Trigger: covenants restored, sweep ceases, accumulated funds release (sometimes immediately, sometimes over months). Sweep structure is heavily negotiated; sophisticated Sponsors get carefully delimited triggers and clear release mechanics.

plain: A Commercial loan structure that's non-recourse until a triggering event occurs — then 'springs' into recourse against the guarantor Sponsor.
snappy: Non-recourse loan that springs into recourse after specified triggering events.
detail: Springing Recourse is the structural framework that holds Bad-Boy Carve-Outs. The loan documents Section 1 declares the loan non-recourse. Section 2 enumerates triggers that 'spring' the loan into full or partial recourse. The Sponsor signs a springing guaranty — a guarantee that's contingent on triggers occurring. Until triggered, the Sponsor's personal assets are protected. After trigger, the Lender can pursue full recourse remedies (judgments, deficiency claims, asset attachment). Springing-guaranty enforcement is heavily litigated — Sponsors argue triggers weren't met, Lenders argue triggers were intentional bad-faith acts. CMBS Special Servicer enforcement of springing recourse generated thousands of disputes 2010-2014.

plain: An automatic fire suppression system — water pipes with heat-activated sprinkler heads — required by code in most commercial buildings, increasingly in residential.
snappy: Automatic fire suppression with heat-activated sprinkler heads.
detail: Sprinkler Systems are mandatory in: most commercial buildings, Multifamily of 3+ stories (varies by state), all new high-rise residential (since 1989 IBC), single-family in some jurisdictions (California new construction since 2011). Sprinkler types: wet-pipe (water always in pipes), dry-pipe (pressurised air, fills with water on activation), pre-action (combination), deluge (open heads). ESFR sprinklers (Early Suppression Fast Response) common in modern Industrial. Cost: $1-$8 PSF retrofit; less for new construction. Insurance discounts: 10-30% on commercial property insurance with full sprinkler coverage.

plain: A property that has reached its target Occupancy Rate and steady-state Operating Expenses — the point where Cap Rates and NOI become meaningful.
snappy: Property at target Occupancy Rate and normalised Operating Expenses — fit for Cap Rate analysis.
detail: Stabilisation matters for both underwriting and lending. A newly developed Multifamily property typically takes 12-24 months to stabilise; commercial Office can take longer. Pre-stabilisation, NOI is depressed by Lease-up vacancy and ramping operating costs — so Cap Rate analysis distorts. Construction Loans usually convert to permanent financing only after a stabilisation hurdle (debt-service coverage, occupancy threshold). Acquisition underwriting often projects 'going-in' NOI off Stabilized assumptions, even if current operations haven't reached them.

plain: The practice of furnishing and arranging a home — often with rented furniture and decor — to maximise its appeal to buyers and Sale Price.
snappy: Furnishing and arranging a home to maximise buyer appeal and Sale Price.
detail: Home Staging has become a standard residential listing practice in many markets. Approaches: full Staging (rental furniture installed by professional Stager), partial Staging (existing furniture rearranged), virtual Staging (digital furniture added to photos). Cost: $500-$5,000+ for partial; $2,000-$15,000+ for full home Staging over 30-90 days. ROI: median-priced homes see 5-10% Sale Price lift on Staged listings; vacant unstaged homes often Sale at meaningful discount. Major Staging companies: Vacant Home Pros, Showhomes, Meridith Baer. Higher-end markets (luxury, urban condo) almost always Stage.

plain: A statutory time limit for filing legal claims — varies by claim type and state — typically 1-10 years from claim accrual or discovery.
snappy: Statutory time limit for filing legal claims — 1-10 years typically.
detail: Statute of Limitations governs Real Estate claims. Typical limits: contract claims (4-6 years), tort claims (1-4 years), fraud claims (2-5 years from discovery), construction defects (4-10 years, varying state). Discovery rule: some claims accrue when discovered rather than when occurring (fraud, latent defects, sexual misconduct). Tolling: some events pause the clock (Tenant in possession, fraud concealment, minority of plaintiff). Real Estate-specific issues: Mortgage Foreclosure deadlines, Mechanic's Lien filing deadlines, Property Tax sale redemption periods. Statute of Limitations distinct from Statute of Repose (absolute time bar regardless of discovery).

plain: A statutory time limit — typically 6-12 years from Substantial Completion — barring construction-defect lawsuits regardless of when the defect was discovered.
snappy: Statutory time bar on construction-defect lawsuits, measured from Substantial Completion.
detail: Statute of Repose imposes absolute time bars distinct from Statute of Limitations. Statute of Limitations: time from defect discovery to filing claim (often 2-4 years). Statute of Repose: time from Substantial Completion to filing claim (typically 6-12 years, varies by state). Even if a buyer discovers a major Latent Defect 15 years after construction, Statute of Repose bars the claim against GC, Subcontractors, or design professionals in most cases. State variations: California 10 years, Texas 10 years (residential), Florida 7 years, Massachusetts 6 years. Critics argue Statute of Repose unfairly disadvantages buyers facing latent defects in older construction.

plain: The defaulted borrower's right — under state statute — to repurchase the property after Foreclosure Sale by paying the auction price plus statutory Interest, available in most Judicial Foreclosure states.
snappy: Borrower's statutory right to repurchase property after Foreclosure Sale by paying auction price plus Interest.
detail: Statutory Redemption is the state-statute extension of Equitable Redemption past the moment of Sale. State laws vary widely. Available in most Judicial Foreclosure states (Illinois, Iowa, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Michigan, etc.); not in most Non-Judicial Foreclosure states (California, Texas). Redemption period: 3 months to 1 year depending on state. The borrower (sometimes junior Lien holders) can repurchase by paying the auction sale price plus statutory Interest (often 10-12%), restoring ownership. Redemption rights create uncertain post-Sale ownership periods — buyers at Foreclosure Sales discount their bids accordingly.

plain: An illegal Real Estate Agent practice of guiding Buyers toward or away from neighbourhoods based on protected characteristics — race, family status, religion.
snappy: Illegal Agent practice of channeling Buyers toward or away from areas by protected class.
detail: Steering violates the Fair Housing Act. Examples: telling a Black Buyer that 'they'd be more comfortable' in one neighbourhood, declining to show listings outside a stereotyped 'family' or 'retiree' area, characterising school quality by demographic proxy. Steering can be subtle and is hard to prove — NAR ethics training emphasises identical service regardless of perceived characteristics. Newsday's 2019 fair-housing investigation in Long Island and subsequent enforcement actions revived public attention. Brokerages train and audit to manage liability.

plain: The opposite of Step-up in Basis — heirs receive property worth less than the deceased's Cost Basis — basis steps down to fair-market value, locking in the loss.
snappy: Opposite of Step-up — basis lowered to fair-market value, locking in a loss.
detail: Step-Down in Basis matters in deflated-market estates. If the deceased purchased at $400,000 and the property is worth $300,000 at death, the heir takes a $300,000 basis — losing the $100,000 unrealised loss that would have been deductible if the deceased had sold before death. Strategic planning: in declining markets, accelerating Sales before death to realise losses can outperform step-down. Estate planners run Sale-versus-Hold sensitivity analyses on appreciated and depreciated assets near end of life.

plain: A tax rule that resets a property's cost basis to its market value at the owner's death — heirs sell with little or no Capital Gain.
snappy: Reset of property's tax basis to fair market value at the owner's death.
detail: Step-up in basis is one of the largest tax breaks in US Real Estate. Heirs inherit at fair market value at date of death; if they sell shortly after, Capital Gain is minimal. A property bought for $200,000 forty years ago and worth $1.2M at owner's death gets stepped up to $1.2M basis — the heir avoids tax on $1M of appreciation. Community Property states grant a full step-up on both halves at the death of one spouse; common-law states grant only half-step-up. Political pressure to limit or eliminate step-up has not (through 2024) produced major reform.

plain: Traditional Single-Family or low-rise construction using individual wood studs framed on-site — distinct from Modular Construction (factory-built) or Panelised Construction.
snappy: Traditional on-site wood-frame construction using individual studs.
detail: Stick-Built dominates US Single-Family residential construction. Workers frame each wall, floor, and roof piece-by-piece on-site using 2x4 or 2x6 studs and beams. Pros: maximum design flexibility, well-understood by every contractor, easy field changes during construction. Cons: weather delays (rain, freeze), inconsistent quality based on crew skill, longer build cycle (8-14 months for typical Custom Home), more waste. Multi-family up to 4-5 storeys can be Stick-Built (Type V); above that, fire codes require steel or concrete. Skill labour shortages have made Stick-Built timelines unpredictable in many markets.

plain: An obsolete Foreclosure form where the court orders Title directly to the Lender without any public sale — survives only in Connecticut and Vermont.
snappy: Court-ordered Title transfer to Lender without public Sale — Connecticut and Vermont only.
detail: Strict Foreclosure was the original English form of Foreclosure — direct Title transfer to the Lender after Default and a court-ordered cure deadline. Almost every US state replaced it with sale-based Judicial Foreclosure or Non-Judicial Foreclosure in the 19th century, where a public auction at least gives the borrower a chance to recover any equity above the loan balance. Connecticut and Vermont retain Strict Foreclosure as the default — the court enters judgment, sets a deadline (typically 1-6 months), and at deadline expiration Title transfers to the Lender. No auction, no public sale, no recovery of equity for the borrower. Connecticut courts occasionally exercise discretion to convert Strict Foreclosure to Foreclosure by sale.

plain: A small Retail centre — typically 5-15 inline shops in a single row with shared parking in front — anchored or unanchored, suburban or urban edge.
snappy: Small linear Retail centre of 5-15 inline shops with shared front parking.
detail: Strip Centers are the dominant suburban Retail format. Unanchored strips: no major Tenant, foot traffic driven by individual destination Tenants. Anchored strips: typically a grocery or drugstore (CVS, Walgreens) anchoring 5-10 inline Tenants. Power strips: junior anchors (Marshalls, Five Below) instead of full grocery. Strip Center Cap Rates trade wider than Class A Mall or community Retail — typically 6.5-8% for stabilised — reflecting smaller Tenant credit, smaller absolute deal sizes, and more disparate ownership pool. National-platform Retail buyers (Phillips Edison, Brixmor) consolidated strip-Retail ownership through the 2010s.

plain: Multifamily property purpose-built for university students — typically rented by the bed rather than the unit, leased to match the academic calendar.
snappy: Multifamily property built for and rented by the bed to university students.
detail: Student housing operates on a unique cycle. Pre-leasing begins in fall for the following academic year; near-full occupancy expected by spring for August move-in. Rent is quoted per bed, with shared common areas and bedrooms inside units. Parents typically co-sign or guarantee, lifting credit risk. Returns track university enrollment trends — Power 5 schools with strong enrollment growth attract institutional capital; mid-tier schools face structural decline. American Campus Communities and Education Realty Trust built the listed REIT sector; Blackstone took ACC private in 2022 for $13B.

plain: A specialty trade firm hired by the General Contractor to perform a specific portion of the work — plumbing, electrical, HVAC, framing, drywall, finishes.
snappy: Specialty trade firm hired by GC for specific work — plumbing, electrical, HVAC, framing.
detail: Subcontractors hold trade-specific licences and perform the discrete pieces of construction. Common subs: framing, plumbing, electrical, HVAC, drywall, painting, flooring, roofing, glazing, concrete, masonry, landscaping, low-voltage. Subs sign sub-contracts with the GC, not directly with the owner. Subs file mechanic's Lien against the property if unpaid by the GC — even if the owner paid the GC in full. Lien waivers from subs at each progress payment protect the owner. Sub default and bonding requirements are major GC risk-management areas.

plain: When a Tenant rents the property out to someone else for part or all of the remaining Lease term.
snappy: Tenant's rental of the leased premises to a third party for some or all of the term.
detail: The Tenant remains liable to the Landlord under the original Lease, while the subtenant pays the original Tenant. Most leases require Landlord consent for sublease, sometimes with reasonable-consent standards (especially commercial) or absolute discretion (typical residential). Assignment, by contrast, transfers the whole Lease — original Tenant exits entirely. Commercial sublease is common when companies downsize but face long remaining terms; rent gap (sublease rent below contract rent) is the original Tenant's loss to bear.

plain: Installing individual utility meters at each rental unit — water, electricity, gas — to bill Tenants for actual consumption rather than including utilities in Rent or using RUBS.
snappy: Installing individual utility meters at each rental unit for actual-use billing.
detail: Submetering competes with RUBS as utility-cost recovery. Investment: $150-$500 per unit for water submetering, more for electric or gas where utility company sub-meters available. Payback: 18-36 months at typical consumption levels. Tenant behaviour: 15-25% utility-cost reduction post-submetering as Tenants modify usage. State regulations: some states (Texas, Colorado, Arizona) explicitly permit submetering with consumer-protection rules; others (California for older properties) restrict. Conservation drives submetering as much as revenue recovery — increasing utility costs and water scarcity make submetering an ESG metric for Sponsor reporting.

plain: A contract by which a Lender or other claim holder agrees its claim ranks below another claim — letting a new senior Mortgage take priority over a pre-existing junior Lien.
snappy: Contract agreeing one claim ranks below another — letting new senior debt take priority.
detail: Subordination Agreements rearrange Capital Stack priority. Common use: a homeowner with a first Mortgage and a HELOC wants to refinance the first Mortgage. Without subordination, the refinance would pay off the first Mortgage but the HELOC would rise to first position — unacceptable to the new Lender. The HELOC Lender signs a Subordination Agreement keeping its position behind the new first Mortgage. Commercial Real Estate uses subordinations extensively in Mezzanine, Preferred Equity, and multi-Lender structures. Junior Lenders charge subordination fees ($500-$5,000+) and may negotiate additional protections (Tenant non-disturbance, intercreditor terms).

plain: The Lender's or Insurer's right to step into the shoes of the party they paid — pursuing third-party recoveries against those at fault.
snappy: Right to step into another party's claim and pursue recovery — used by Insurers and Lenders.
detail: Subrogation appears across Real Estate finance. Title Insurance: insurer pays a claim, then subrogates against the party responsible for the Title Defect (fraudulent grantor, negligent attorney, prior owner). Mortgage: Lender pays off a senior Lien to preserve security, then subrogates to that senior Lien's position rather than losing priority. Homeowners Insurance: insurer pays a fire-damage claim, subrogates against the negligent contractor whose work caused the fire. Subrogation rights are typically built into policies and contracts. Without subrogation, Insurers and Lenders would bear losses that should fall on third parties.

plain: The construction milestone when the building can be used for its intended purpose — even if minor punch-list items remain — triggers Lease commencement, warranty periods, and final-payment milestones.
snappy: Construction milestone: building usable for intended purpose; triggers Lease and warranty clocks.
detail: Substantial Completion is the critical contractual moment in any construction project. The architect issues a Certificate of Substantial Completion when the building can serve its intended use — Tenants can occupy, warehouses can operate. Punch List items may remain but the building works. Substantial Completion triggers: Lease Rent commencement, Tenant Improvement reimbursement, warranty-period start, Mechanic's Lien deadline, owner take-over for insurance and operations. Final Completion follows weeks-to-months later after punch-list completion. Disputes over Substantial Completion are common — contract definitions vary, and the trigger involves real money for the owner, GC, and Tenants.

plain: A Tenant's voluntary giving-up of the leased premises before Lease expiration — typically by mutual agreement with the Landlord, often involving payment of remaining Rent or other consideration.
snappy: Tenant voluntary giving-up of leased premises before Lease expiration.
detail: Surrender lets Tenants exit Leases early with Landlord consent. Mechanics: Tenant proposes surrender terms; Landlord negotiates payment for early termination, often equal to remaining Rent or some discount. Landlord motivation to accept: gain control of space sooner, re-lease at higher market rate, redevelopment plans. Tenant motivation to surrender: business closure, downsizing, relocation. Surrender agreements should explicitly address: Security Deposit return, ongoing repair obligations, condition of premises on surrender, post-surrender confidentiality. Distinguish from abandonment (Tenant leaves without consent — usually treated as Default).

plain: A professional measurement of property boundaries, structures, and Easements — produces a drawing used at Closing and for new construction.
snappy: Boundary and improvement measurement of a property by a licensed surveyor.
detail: Surveys come in flavours of precision. A boundary survey marks the property lines (corner monuments, dimensions). An ALTA/NSPS Land Title Survey is the institutional standard for commercial transactions — boundary plus structures, Easements, encroachments, flood zone, and improvements. A mortgage location survey is cheaper, used for residential refi. Lenders often require a current survey at Closing. Surveys surface Encroachments, missing setbacks, and unrecorded Easements that Title Insurance might otherwise miss.

plain: A private buyer acquires a listed REIT and takes it off the public exchange — typically at a premium to NAV when listed REITs trade at deep discounts.
snappy: Private acquisition of a listed REIT, removing it from public markets.
detail: Take-private transactions accelerated in 2020-2023 as listed REITs traded at discounts to private-market values. Notable deals: Blackstone's $13B take-private of American Campus Communities (2022), Blackstone + Starwood take-private of Extended Stay (2021), Brookfield's take-private of various asset-heavy REITs. Mechanics: cash tender offer typically 15-30% premium to undisturbed share price, board-and-shareholder approval, regulatory clearance. Once private, the REIT loses public-market liquidity but gains operational flexibility and avoids quarterly reporting pressure. The 2024 listed REIT recovery softened the take-private opportunity but didn't close it entirely.

plain: A public-finance mechanism that earmarks future Property Tax revenue growth — within a designated district — to fund infrastructure or Development incentives in that district.
snappy: Public-finance mechanism using future Property Tax growth to fund district infrastructure.
detail: Tax Increment Financing (TIF) emerged 1950s and spread to 49 US states. Mechanics: city designates a 'TIF district' with a baseline Property Tax revenue. Future increases in Property Tax revenue (the 'tax increment') get diverted to fund infrastructure or Development incentives within the district rather than to general municipal budget. Common uses: brownfield redevelopment, downtown revitalisation, transit-oriented Development, infrastructure to support new Multifamily. Controversies: TIF diverts revenue from schools and county services for decades; some TIF projects have failed financially leaving taxpayer obligations. Chicago, St. Louis, Atlanta among heaviest US TIF users.

plain: A government Lien on a property for unpaid Property Tax — has Senior priority over other Liens, often higher than even first Mortgages.
snappy: Government Lien for unpaid Property Tax — Senior priority above most other Liens.
detail: Tax Liens are the most-senior claim against Real Property in nearly every state. Failure to pay Property Tax triggers a Tax Lien automatically; counties then either auction the Lien to investors (Florida, Arizona, Iowa) or take the property for Tax Deed sale (California, Texas, Pennsylvania). Tax Lien investors earn statutory Interest — often 12-18% APR — until the homeowner redeems. Tax Lien sales attract capital seeking yield but require disciplined Due Diligence — most Liens redeem before maturity; the few that don't can produce property acquisition at deep discount to market.

plain: Affordable Housing financing using federal tax-exempt municipal bonds — paired with 4% LIHTC credits to fund construction of below-market-rent housing.
snappy: Affordable Housing financing using federal tax-exempt bonds plus 4% LIHTC credits.
detail: Tax-Exempt Bond Financing pairs with the 4% LIHTC program for Affordable Housing Development. State housing finance agency issues tax-exempt private-activity bonds; investors accept lower yields (federal income-tax-exempt); developer uses proceeds for construction or rehabilitation; LIHTC investors purchase 4% credits to provide additional equity. State-level bond cap is set by federal allocation; demand routinely exceeds supply. This approach has surged post-2010.

plain: The 2017 federal tax law that cut corporate rates, capped the state and local tax deduction, and reshaped Real Estate tax treatment.
snappy: 2017 federal tax overhaul affecting depreciation, 1031 Exchange scope, and the SALT deduction.
detail: TCJA's Real Estate impacts run wide. Mortgage interest deduction was capped at $750,000 of acquisition debt (down from $1M); HELOC interest only deductible for substantial improvements. State and Local Tax (SALT) deduction capped at $10,000 — devastating in high-Property-Tax states. Section 199A pass-through deduction extended to qualified Real Estate businesses. Bonus Depreciation expanded to 100% then phasing down to zero by 2027. 1031 Exchange restricted to Real Property only; personal-property exchanges eliminated.

plain: The right and condition of holding property as a Tenant under a Lease — also the collective term for the various co-ownership forms (Joint Tenancy, Tenancy in Common, Tenancy by the Entirety).
snappy: Right or condition of holding property as Tenant — also the collective term for co-ownership forms.
detail: Two distinct senses share the word. (1) Leasehold tenancy: the Tenant's possessory right under a Lease — periodic (month-to-month), term (fixed Lease), sufferance (Holdover Tenant), at will. (2) Co-ownership tenancy: the umbrella for Joint Tenancy, Tenancy in Common, and Tenancy by the Entirety — the various forms of multi-owner Title. Context disambiguates. The shared root makes sense — both senses describe the right of holding, just from different angles (occupying versus owning).

plain: A form of joint ownership available only to married couples — strongest creditor protection of any co-ownership form.
snappy: Marital co-ownership form with right of survivorship and joint-creditor protection.
detail: Recognised in roughly half the states (Florida, New York, Ohio, Massachusetts among them). Tenancy by the Entirety requires marriage and treats the spouses as a single legal entity owning the property. A creditor of just one spouse cannot reach the property — creditors of both can. Right of survivorship at death is automatic. Divorce typically converts Tenancy by the Entirety to Tenancy in Common. The structure is favoured for primary-residence asset protection where state law allows.

plain: Two or more owners hold the property together — but each share passes to the owner's heirs at death, not to the co-owners.
snappy: Co-ownership where each share is independently inheritable and transferable.
detail: Tenancy in common is the default form when a Deed conveys to multiple buyers without specifying Joint Tenancy. Shares can be unequal (60/40, 70/30) and each owner can sell or will their interest independently. Common in investment partnerships and unmarried co-buyers. No survivorship — a deceased owner's share goes through Probate to heirs, who become new co-tenants. Co-tenants share rights to possess the whole property, regardless of percentage ownership.

plain: Ownership of property by a single individual or entity — the simplest form of Title, distinct from any co-ownership.
snappy: Sole ownership by a single individual or entity — the simplest Title form.
detail: Tenancy in Severalty (sometimes 'sole ownership' or 'individual ownership') is the default when a Deed names only one grantee. Single individuals, single corporations, single LLCs all hold Title in severalty. The single owner makes all decisions, faces all liability, and inherits/wills the property without co-ownership complications. Sole ownership simplifies estate planning (only one estate to probate) but lacks the survivorship benefits of Joint Tenancy and Tenancy by the Entirety. Spouses sometimes hold in severalty to preserve separate-property classification in community-property states.

plain: The person or business renting a property under a Lease — pays Rent, follows the rules, has the right to possess the space.
snappy: Person or entity occupying leased property in exchange for Rent.
detail: Tenants get rights that pre-empt many private contract terms. The right to a habitable dwelling, quiet enjoyment, security-deposit protection, and proper Eviction procedure all flow from state and (in some cities) local statute. Commercial tenants have weaker statutory rights — they negotiate protections into the Lease. Subleases let a tenant transfer occupancy to a third party, usually with Landlord consent. Holdover tenants who stay past lease expiration become month-to-month or trigger Eviction depending on Landlord response.

plain: A Tenant's formal exercise of Lease Audit Right — examination of Landlord's Operating Expense and CAM books to verify accuracy of pass-through charges.
snappy: Tenant exercise of Lease Audit Right — examination of Landlord's CAM books.
detail: Tenant Audit converts the Audit Right from a Lease provision into actual examination. Process: Tenant retains an audit specialist (CPA firm, specialised Lease audit firms like Real Estate Audit Group, Optical Realty), submits formal audit notice to Landlord, Landlord provides records (typically within 30-60 days of request). Audit duration: 30-180 days. Common findings: ineligible expenses included in CAM, capital improvements wrongly classified as operating, management-fee overpayments. Recovery: Tenant credit for overcharges plus, if overcharge exceeds Lease-defined threshold, Landlord pays audit costs. Tenant Audit waves occur during soft markets.

plain: A signed Tenant statement confirming Lease terms — required at Sale or refinance of Commercial property — letting the buyer or Lender rely on the disclosed Lease facts.
snappy: Tenant signed statement confirming Lease terms at Sale or refinance.
detail: Tenant Estoppels are part of every institutional Commercial Real Estate transaction. The Tenant confirms: current Rent and how calculated, term remaining, options and renewal rights, no Landlord defaults, no Tenant offsets or claims, no oral side agreements, no pending litigation. Estoppel binds the Tenant — they cannot later assert facts contrary to what they signed. Lease typically requires Tenant to provide Estoppel within 10-30 days of Landlord request; failure can be Landlord-favourable Default. Major Tenants negotiate Estoppel format and timing carefully. Lender refusal to fund commonly cited reason: missing or qualified estoppels from major Tenants.

plain: Money the Landlord spends — or credits the Tenant for — to customise a leased space before the Tenant moves in.
snappy: Landlord allowance or work funding interior customisation of leased space for a Tenant.
detail: TI dollars are heavily negotiated in Commercial Lease economics. The Landlord typically offers a per-square-foot allowance ($25-$150 PSF depending on market and Lease length) to fund Tenant-specific Build-Out — partitions, finishes, mechanical changes, IT cabling. The TI investment is amortised into the base Rent or treated as Lease-level Capital Expenditure by the Landlord. Long Leases justify higher TI; short Leases get little or none. Unused TI typically reverts to the Landlord.

plain: A specific dollar-per-square-foot amount the Landlord agrees to spend or contribute toward building out the Tenant's space — heavily negotiated in commercial Lease economics.
snappy: Specific dollar-per-square-foot amount Landlord contributes toward Tenant Build-Out.
detail: TI Allowance translates Lease economics into upfront capital. Range: $25-$150 PSF for Office, $20-$80 PSF for Retail, $5-$30 PSF for Industrial — varying by market, Lease length, and Tenant credit. Long Leases justify higher TIA; short Leases get little. Method: the Landlord either pays for the Build-Out directly (turnkey) or reimburses the Tenant up to the TIA limit (Tenant-built TI). Unused TIA usually reverts to the Landlord. TI Allowance is amortised into Base Rent over the Lease term — effectively a Landlord loan paid back by the Tenant through above-market Rent. NER calculation nets TIA off the headline Rent.

plain: Insurance the Tenant carries — typically required by Lease — covering Tenant's personal property and liability for damage to the leased premises or Co-Tenants.
snappy: Tenant's required insurance covering personal property and liability for damage.
detail: Tenant Insurance is Lease-required in nearly all institutional Multifamily and most commercial Leases. Residential Renter Insurance: covers Tenant's personal property and personal liability (slip-and-fall guests, dog bites, water damage to neighbours). Coverage typically $30K-$100K, premiums $10-$30/month. Commercial Tenant Insurance: CGL with Landlord as additional insured, plus business personal property coverage. Lease provisions require Tenant to maintain insurance and provide certificates to Landlord annually. Tenant failures to maintain coverage can trigger Lease Default. Some Landlords offer master Tenant insurance bundled into Rent.

plain: Texas's strong constitutional protection of a primary residence — caps Property Tax assessment growth, shields against most creditor claims, restricts forced sale.
snappy: Texas constitutional protection of primary residence — tax cap, creditor shield, forced-sale restriction.
detail: Texas Homestead protections sit in Article XVI of the Texas Constitution. Three layers. Property Tax: assessed value growth on a primary residence capped at 10% per year through the Homestead exemption, plus a $40,000 (or higher) reduction in taxable value. Creditor protection: the homestead cannot be reached by most unsecured creditors — federal tax liens and Mortgages can; credit-card debt and most lawsuits cannot. Forced sale: severely restricted — only for Property Tax, Mortgage, mechanic's lien for improvements, or home-equity loans. The protection makes Texas a popular asset-protection state.

plain: A Real Estate financing technique using a Mortgage with both an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage feature and a Fixed-Rate component — also a slang for certain Foreclosure-defence tactics.
snappy: Slang for both a multi-tranche Texas Mortgage structure and a Texas Foreclosure-defence tactic.
detail: Two senses share the name. (1) Mortgage structure: a hybrid Loan with both fixed-rate Principal and a variable-rate component, popular in Texas in the 2000s.
